# Welcome to EITR

EITR combines an Arch Linux system, Hyprland windows, the Quickshell desktop bar
and Walker menus. **SUPER** means the Windows/Command-logo key on your keyboard.

The buttons above this text set up the essentials: each one closes the handbook
and opens its setting. This chapter opens by itself at the first login; turn on
**Show this welcome at the next login** to see it again, or reopen it any time
from **Learn > Welcome**.

**Offer to report problems when something breaks** is on by default and shares the Crash Notifications setting. When one of your programs crashes, a notification offers help or a report for you to review and send; see [Troubleshooting](handbook:troubleshooting).

## Your first few minutes

1. Press **SUPER + F** for the main menu. Start typing to search actions across
   submenus and installed apps. Enter opens a result; Escape closes the menu.
2. Press **SUPER + Space** for Apps, or **SUPER + Enter** for a terminal.
3. Open **SUPER + ,** for the Control Center. Its Settings tab contains keyboard
   and display/night-light controls; Style contains appearance choices.
4. Connect from the WiFi or Bluetooth icon. Right-side bar icons may be hidden:
   click the Show Icons arrow to reveal them.
5. Choose a theme from **Style > Theme**, then a wallpaper from **Style > Wallpaper**.

Fresh EITR defaults are **Afterglow** and the **Clockwork Tape** lockscreen.
Existing desktops keep their saved choices.

## Learn at your own pace

Open **Learn > EITR Handbook** or press **SUPER + F1**. Press the same shortcut
again, Escape, or the close button to dismiss this overlay; clicking beside it
keeps it open. It does not tile beside your apps. Search matches chapter titles and text;
Up/Down pick a match and Enter opens it. **Ctrl + F** focuses search.
**Page Up/Page Down** scroll the chapter, **Ctrl + Home/End** jump to its start
or end, and **Alt + Left/Right** moves between chapters. Previous and Next do
the same with the mouse.

The handbook does not run commands. Code blocks are examples for you to inspect
and copy deliberately. External reference links open only when clicked.

Continue with [Shortcuts](handbook:shortcuts),
[Desktop Bar](handbook:desktop-bar), or the [System Menu](handbook:system).

# Git accounts

Open **Development > Git Accounts**. GitHub and GitLab accounts can be used
simultaneously, including several accounts on the same provider or enterprise
hostname. GitHub CLI (`gh`) and GitLab CLI (`glab`) ship in new installations.
Existing ISO images must be rebuilt to include changes.

Each account is a row showing where Git uses it: **Default**, the names of its
folders, or **Not used yet**. Press Enter on an account to open its actions;
Shift+Backspace returns to the list.

## First setup

1. **Add Account** opens the shared step-by-step form for provider, account name, commit author name and email, hostname, an optional existing private SSH key, default identity and folder rule. Every answer appears in Review; revisit any step before applying. Esc or Ctrl+C cancels without saving.
2. **Import Existing Setup** reads identities configured by hand instead: the
   default `user.name`/`user.email` and per-folder `includeIf "gitdir:…"` rules in
   `~/.gitconfig` or `~/.config/git/config`, including the SSH alias and key an
   included file routes through (`url.<alias>.insteadOf`). It lists what it found
   and creates matching accounts and rules after confirmation. Your files stay
   unchanged; wildcard folder patterns are listed as skipped.

## Default and folders

The **default** account applies in every folder without its own account. A
**folder** account applies only to repositories inside that folder. The most
specific folder wins; repository-local settings and Git command-line or
environment overrides still take precedence. EITR preserves existing global
configuration and comments, adding a marked include at the end of
`~/.gitconfig`, and confirmed rules override identities from external includes.

Account actions in Walker, each confirmed before saving and reported in a
notification: **Make Default** or **Stop Using as Default**, **Add Folder**
(pick `~/Development` or a folder inside it, or **Other folder…** to type a
path) and **Remove Folder**. Git matches the actual `.git` directory, so linked
worktrees and submodules can follow a parent repository's account.

## SSH keys

Commit identity does not grant repository access. **Show Public Key** prints the
account's public key, copies it to the clipboard and names the provider page to
add it to (GitHub: Settings > SSH keys). **Set Existing SSH Key** picks a key
from `~/.ssh`; **Create SSH Key** makes an Ed25519 key with a passphrase and then
shows its public key. **Test Connection** reports the provider's greeting, such
as "Hi username!", in a notification. Never share a private key.

Keys apply only to their provider SSH hostname. The launcher resolves existing
SSH aliases without connecting, then uses only the selected key, ignoring other
SSH configuration for that connection. Proxy connections are refused; retain a
repository-local `core.sshCommand` for advanced setups. Known-host verification
stays enabled. Accounts without a configured key use normal SSH, not another
account's key. HTTPS credentials and credential helpers are unchanged.

## Provider CLIs

**Log In to CLI** signs into a separate config directory for each account; it
does not switch the ordinary global `gh` or `glab` account. Inherited
provider-token variables are removed for that process. Its confirmation explains
that tokens are stored in private, unencrypted CLI profile files, avoiding
keyring entries shared between accounts on the same host.
Never share `~/.config/eitr/git-accounts/cli`; it is not included in EITR backups.

From a repository, use the account-aware CLI:

```sh
eitr-git cli auth status
eitr-git cli repo view
```

The selected default/folder account chooses `gh` or `glab`. Ordinary CLI commands
keep their existing global behavior. SSH-key registration does not authenticate
CLI API operations. No Bitbucket CLI is bundled.

## Removal and recovery

**Edit Name and Email** changes identity fields; **Remove Account** removes an
account and its rules after confirmation. Removing a folder rule falls back to a
broader rule or the default; clearing the default restores existing Git settings
outside remaining rules. Projects, keys and CLI credentials are never deleted,
and removing a rule does not revoke provider access.

Versioned settings live in `~/.config/eitr/git-accounts.json`. Every apply backs
up the global Git file, active include and settings under
`~/.local/state/eitr/git-account-backups/<id>` with private permissions.
`manifest.json` identifies original paths, backup filenames and modes. Keys and
CLI tokens are never copied. For manual recovery, review that manifest and keep
any edits made since the backup before restoring files. Edited or malformed
EITR include blocks are refused instead of silently replaced.

References: [Git conditional includes](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config),
[GitHub CLI profiles](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_help_environment),
[GitLab CLI profiles](https://docs.gitlab.com/cli/configuration/).

# Desktop bar and workspaces

The bar keeps the date and time centered. Its left side contains Overview,
workspace markers, Hardware, AI Usage and Idle Lock; its right side contains device/status
controls. Click **Show Icons** to reveal or hide that right-side group.

## Updates

The updates icon in the right-side group, before Notifications, checks for
package and AUR updates shortly after you log in and every six hours. When it
finds new updates, a notification offers to run System Update. It spins while checking,
then shows a check mark when the system is up to date, or an update icon whose
tooltip gives the number of updates and the download size. Click it to run
System Update; right-click it to check again. It checks again automatically when
System Update finishes. When offline, it shows up to date and checks again at
the next login. The check uses a private copy of the package databases, so it
never leaves the system partially upgraded.

## Position and appearance

- Double-left-click **empty bar space** to switch Blur/Theme Color (new
  installations start with Theme Color).
- Double-right-click empty space to switch the full bar/centered hover layout.
- Drag empty space toward the top, bottom, left or right to move the bar.
- The same settings are under **Style > Desktop Bar** and Control Center > Style.
- **Displays** (Show on) puts the bar on the main display only, the default, or
  on every display. With a bar on every display, each one marks the workspace
  shown on its own screen, shortcuts such as SUPER + , open on the display you
  are using, and notifications pop up on the main display only. Choose the
  main display in the Display panel.

Centered mode shows the clock until you hover. Icons unfold in their usual
order. The pin between media and the clock keeps the bar open; open panels
also keep it expanded. Full-bar panels join the bar; centered-bar panels sit
beside it. Both open and close with the same fluid animation.

## Workspaces

The bar starts with 1–5 and expands through the current/highest occupied
workspace, up to 10. Empty higher markers disappear when no longer needed.
Right-click a marker to choose Dots, Glyph, Numbers or Runes, with live examples.
Runes is the default.
Runes shows workspaces 1 to 10 as the first ten Elder Futhark runes (ᚠ ᚢ ᚦ ᚨ ᚱ
ᚲ ᚷ ᚹ ᚺ ᚾ).

**SUPER + 1–9/0** switches workspace; **SUPER + Shift + 1–9/0** moves a window.
**SUPER + Tab** opens Overview. Click a preview or use arrows and Enter;
1–9/0 switches directly. Only occupied numbered workspaces appear, and their
previews stay in memory. Escape/outside click closes Overview.

**SUPER + S** toggles the special workspace, which is separate from Overview.
**SUPER + Shift + Space** hides/shows the bar, not the notification service.

On empty desktop space, the wallpaper/theme mouse gestures are listed under
**Learn > Mouse Gestures**. Use the keyboard carousel shortcuts when in doubt.

The Audio/Mic control opens one panel with separate output and microphone sections. Tailscale and Streaming sit immediately before OBS. A switch in their header connects Tailscale or starts sharing, details and devices follow, and setup or diagnostic actions are in the "…" menu. Icon buttons show their background on hover; panels refresh by themselves when they open, a refresh icon spins only while they load, and tooltips appear near the pointer. Switches and inset action buttons use compact shared sizes.

# Control Center

Press **SUPER + ,** to toggle the Control Center. It opens from the bar's current
edge and closes on Escape or an outside click. Closing returns it to General.

Its four pages hold everything outside Development, Apps, Install, Learn and
Gaming, so most settings never need Walker. Folding sections start closed; click
a section's title to open or close it, remembered until you log out. Where the bar has its own panel (OBS, WiFi,
Bluetooth, Audio, Display, Hardware, AI Usage, Weather), the Control Center opens it.

## General

- **Connectivity:** WiFi and Bluetooth power toggles, plus Airplane mode.
- **Quick Toggles:** automatic Idle Lock, Crash Notifications, Do Not Disturb, Game Mode (effects, blur
  and popups off and the performance profile on, until you turn it off) and Night
  Light. A toggle that is on fills with the theme accent. Below them, Hide Bar
  (SUPER+Shift+Space brings it back) and Screensaver run once.
- **Sound:** volume and microphone gain/mute.
- **Display:** brightness.
- **Media:** cover, artist, playback controls and seeking when supported.
- **Power:** Lock, plus **Power…**, which unfolds Logout, Suspend, Reboot and Shutdown.

Airplane mode remembers which radios it blocked and restores only those.
Do Not Disturb suppresses popups without clearing notification history.
Idle Lock is not the same as preventing sleep; be mindful of screen privacy.

## Style

Theme and Wallpaper open their carousels; Default Font opens the font list. The
lockscreen design, cursor (family, size and color), bar appearance, layout,
edge and displays, workspace markers, corners and Kitty's Cursor Fire change right in the
panel and share their preferences with Walker.

## Tools

Screenshots (selection, full screen, window, or a selection straight to the
clipboard), recording (the OBS controls, Record, Record + Audio and Stop), OCR,
QR codes, the color picker, Transcode, reminders and LocalSend sharing. The panel
closes before a selection or recording starts.

## System

- **Devices:** Audio, Microphone, Display (resolution, refresh rate and scale),
  Bluetooth and WiFi panels, Lighting, and the battery charge limit on laptops.
- **Keyboard:** layouts can be selected, added and removed, with at least one kept.
- **Night Light & Main Display:** Night Light's mode and schedule (distinct
  from its manual switch) and the main display, which holds the bar.
- **Information:** About, Hardware, AI Usage, Weather and Report a Problem.

  Pacman-only or AUR-only updates.

  their guide, Cleanup and Dotfiles.

Security settings, factory reset and the network backend stay in Walker > System,
behind their own confirmations.

**System > Language** shows the current language and follows the system locale.
Open the picker to choose a language or System default, then sign out and back
in to apply it. It changes only your user-session message locale, never the
system locale files. See the [Language guide](handbook:language).

# Themes, wallpapers and style

## Themes and wallpapers

Open **Style > Theme** or **SUPER + Ctrl + Shift + N**. Pick Dark/Light, then a
theme. Start typing inside the theme carousel to filter; arrows/Tab move and
Enter applies. Backspace edits search first; Escape clears search before closing.
The category picker and wallpaper carousel do not have theme search.

**SUPER + Ctrl + N** opens wallpapers, and **SUPER + Shift + N** advances to
the next one. A checkmark marks the active choice in Walker. Theme/wallpaper
changes stay quiet: they do not send success notifications. Ultrawide monitors
(at least twice as wide as tall) show each wallpaper's 21:9 version, so less of
the picture is cut away; other monitors show the 4K 16:9 one.

The Norse theme includes drawn raven, Valkyrie, Odin, Fenrir and Jörmungandr
wallpapers on black backgrounds. Select them through these same wallpaper
controls; the additional artwork does not change the palette. Its first
wallpaper, the runestone, is live: the northern lights drift slowly behind the
rune ring. They pause behind fullscreen apps, and the lockscreen shows the still
image.

## Bar and corners

**Style > Desktop Bar** selects Blur/Theme Color, full/centered layout and edge.
Walker follows that appearance. **Style > Corners** selects Square, Rounded or
Extra Rounded for EITR surfaces and compositor decorations. Third-party apps
may retain their own internal widget style; circular status dots remain circular.

## Fonts

**Style > Fonts** lists usable installed font families, not every bold/italic
variant. Document/fallback families stay hidden. JetBrainsMono Nerd Font is
the default. Selection updates supported desktop apps; ligatures are enabled
where supported. Removing a family removes its supported installed variants;
the last usable choice cannot be deleted. Package ownership may require review.

## Cursor

**Style > Cursor** offers Bibata Modern, Breeze and Vanilla DMZ; Color offers
Auto, Dark and Light; Size chooses the pointer size. Auto follows the theme's
light/dark category without changing your selected family. Explicit color
overrides persist. The selected row uses a left-side checkmark; other family
choices show previews. Missing assets produce an error rather than saving a
broken selection.

The Limine boot menu shown at power-on uses the current theme's colours, an
EITR title and a larger font. Fresh installations set this up; after a theme
change the menu follows at the next shutdown, and the default theme's colours
are used if yours cannot be read. Boot entries are never changed, and
`limine.conf` is backed up before each change. The style is skipped while
Secure Boot is enabled, because an enrolled Limine config hash would stop the
system booting after an edit.

**Style > Lockscreen** sets the design of both the lockscreen and the login
screen. Existing preferences survive theme changes.

Available designs are Clockwork Neo Orbital, Clockwork Tape, Girl Coffee,
Girl Pillow, Material Dark, Material Light, Nothing and Theme Wallpaper. Only shipped designs
appear in the picker; previews do not lock the session. A selection of a design
that is no longer shipped moves to Clockwork Tape, the default for fresh
installations.

The artwork targets 4K (3840×2160, 16:9). Coffee and Pillow keep their
relaxed anime style with Norse clothing; Material and Clockwork use subtle rune
ornaments. Nothing keeps its existing design. QML and SVG remain scalable.

Compare the eight shipped EITR designs using
`bash quickshell/lockscreen/scripts/gallery.sh`. This does not change the selected
lockscreen; authentication and power actions are disabled in the gallery.
Clockwork uses procedural QML; Coffee, Pillow, Material and Nothing retain the
licensed layouts with new artwork and installed JetBrainsMono Nerd Font. No
bundled fonts or videos are required.

**Theme Wallpaper** uses the selected desktop wallpaper with a clock at the top
left and password controls at the bottom right. Its Walker preview shows the
current wallpaper. It follows later wallpaper changes at the next lock or
preview; Ctrl+P previews the full layout without locking. The login screen cannot
read your home folder, so it shows a copy of the wallpaper that Eitr stores when
you choose this design and again whenever you change wallpaper. If the saved image
is unavailable it uses another current-theme wallpaper or the Norse default.

chapters.markdown:
# Apps and installation

Before installing official packages, the terminal shows that it is checking for pending system updates. This check may take a while before the administrator password is requested. Flatpak installations also announce their preparation stage.

**SUPER + Space** and Main > Apps open the same app list. Enter launches an app.
Delete is available in Apps and asks for uninstall confirmation. Global search
from **SUPER + F** launches apps but does not expose uninstall actions.
There is no separate pin-based app menu.

Typing in the main menu searches installed apps and actions from all submenus.
Typing inside a submenu, such as System or Install, searches that submenu and
everything below it. Submenu rows end with **>**; **Shift + Backspace** returns
to the parent.

## Install

Press Delete on an installed entry in the named Install lists to uninstall it after confirmation. Web Apps retain their removal action. Packages (Pacman and Yay) remain install-only and have no Delete action. Required system dependencies are never removed recursively; pacman refuses removals that would break another package.

Managed language bundles show their full removal warning in a terminal before asking for confirmation with [y/N]; Enter cancels. Node removal includes all NVM-managed versions and their global npm tools. Python removal affects uv-managed versions and uv, not system Python. Java removes the current SDKMAN Java and Maven versions; Rust removes only its stable toolchain. Rails and Laravel remove their framework tools while retaining Ruby, PHP and Composer. Projects, settings and credentials are kept, but dependent tools and environments may stop working. Native assistant removal keeps cached versions and settings.


Apps already on the system show **Installed** under their name; choosing one
says so instead of installing it again. This also recognizes tools installed by
their own managers, such as Java from SDKMAN or Node.js from NVM. Packages that
need a runtime, such as DBeaver's Java, bring a small one only when no package
provides it yet.

- **AI CLIs:** optional AI command-line clients.
- **Browsers:** supported browser choices.
- **Databases:** optional tools such as DBeaver, database clients and Valkey
  (the Redis-compatible server Arch ships instead of Redis).
- **Development Languages:** optional language toolchains; Java/Flutter are
  not mandatory desktop dependencies.
- **JavaScript Tools:** optional JavaScript runtimes and tooling.
- **Packages > Pacman** and **Packages > Yay (AUR):** search the official Arch
  packages or the community AUR packages, each labeled with where it comes from
  and whether it is installed. The search is on top, the packages under it and
  the selected package's details below; **Ctrl+B** shows its build file
  (PKGBUILD) instead and back, **Ctrl+O** opens its page in the browser, **Tab**
  selects several and **Enter** installs them. AUR packages are built on this
  computer from their build file, so read it first; they are not official Arch
  packages.

Installation/update/setup terminals show the themed EITR banner. Successful
tasks normally close; failures stay visible. Reports such as Cleanup stay open
so you can read them. Ordinary terminals and About do not show the task banner.

Press **Esc** to close waiting task, account, report and About terminals. Enter remains for answers and confirmations, including acknowledging a recovery key and powering off the installer.

## Tools

**Calculator** in Apps (or the keyboard's calculator key) opens Eitr's
calculator in the current theme's colors. Type or click: `+ − × ÷`, `^` for
powers, `%` for percent (`200×15%`), `√` and brackets; a number before a
bracket multiplies (`2(3+4)`). Enter shows the result, Backspace removes a
character, Escape clears (twice closes) and Ctrl+C or **Copy** copies the result.
It works out the expression itself rather than running it as code.

**Offline dictation** is speech-to-text that never leaves the computer. Hold
**SUPER + D**, speak, and release: the words are
typed where the cursor is, in the language you spoke. While it listens, the red
dot beside the weather becomes a small waveform that moves with your voice, so
you can see it hears you; after release it pulses until the words are typed.
The first use downloads the
speech model once (148 MB, checked against its published checksum) to
`~/.local/share/eitr/whisper/`; after that it works offline. Transcribing takes a
moment after release, longer on older processors.

**Main > Tools > Reminders > New Reminder** asks when (a delay such as `10m` or `1h30m`, or a
time of day such as `18:30`) and what about, then shows a notification at that
time that stays until you dismiss it. **Upcoming Reminders** lists the waiting
ones; pick one to cancel it. Reminders survive a restart, and any that came due
while the computer was off appear at the next login. From a terminal:
`eitr remind 25m Take the tea out`, and `eitr remind` alone lists them.

## Gaming

Main > Gaming lists **GeForce NOW**, **RetroArch** and **Steam**. Choosing one
opens it when it is installed, and installs it otherwise. RetroArch comes from
Arch's official packages with cores for the classic consoles: NES, SNES, Game
Boy and Game Boy Advance, Mega Drive/Genesis, PlayStation, Nintendo 64, Nintendo
DS, PSP and Dreamcast. Add your own games and, where a console needs one, its
BIOS files; Eitr ships neither. GeForce NOW installs from Flatpak.

**Toggle > Game Mode** gets the desktop out of the way while you play: window
animations, blur and shadows turn off, notification popups wait (do not
disturb), and the power profile switches to performance where the computer has
one. Turning it off restores exactly what it changed. Steam installs with
**GameMode** and **MangoHud**: add `gamemoderun mangohud %command%` to a game's
launch options in Steam to boost the CPU during play and show the FPS overlay.

LocalSend's packaged app includes its runtime requirements: you do not need
the Flutter SDK just to run it. Developer tools remain optional.

Use [Updates & Cleanup](handbook:maintenance) for upgrading; installing one
package is not the same as the snapshot-protected System Update workflow.

chapters.markdown:
# Finding your way around System

Open **SUPER + F > System**. Actions are grouped alphabetically; global search
still finds them directly, without making you navigate every group.

## Connectivity

**Bluetooth**, **Network Backend**, **WiFi**. The device entries open the same
panels as the bar. Backend selection prepares the next boot, not a live restart.

## Devices & Input

**Audio**, **Battery Charge Limit**, **Display**, **Keyboard**, **Lighting**,
**Microphone**. Charge-limit controls require supported laptop firmware. Display
contains brightness, Night Light, monitor selection and supported laptop power
profiles.

**Lighting** decides whether theme changes recolour fans, keyboards and other
devices that OpenRGB controls. It is off by default, so EITR leaves your
lighting alone; choose **Follow Theme** to give them the theme's colour now and
at every theme change.

## Information

**About**, **AI Usage**, **Hardware**, **Report a Problem**, **Weather**. About
opens the EITR system summary; Report a Problem collects a private report you
read before sending. The others use native panels. Calendar and Workspace Overview remain
available from the bar and global search rather than crowding this menu. Search
for **Ragnarök** to let Fenrir bite the screen; click or Escape ends it early.

## Maintenance

**Cleanup**, **Factory Reset**, **Snapshots**, **Update**. Update separates
System Update from Advanced package updates. Factory Reset is destructive and
requires two warnings; read [Factory Reset](handbook:factory-reset) first.

## Security

**FIDO2 Security Key**, **Fingerprint**, **TPM Disk Unlock**, **Firewall**, **Return
to Password Authentication**, **Update Password**. Secure Boot documentation is in
**Learn > EITR Handbook > Secure Boot**, not a separate menu or security-setting action.

## Dotfiles

Opens your configuration directory in VS Code, or in LazyVim when VS Code is
not installed. Keep machine-specific monitor
and hardware overrides in `~/.config/hypr/local.lua`, not the shared defaults.
Do not paste tokens, recovery keys or passwords into configuration backups.

Use the chapters that follow for the detailed workflows and safety limits.

## Language

**Walker > System > Language** lists the languages, with the current one
checked; see the [Language guide](handbook:language).
English menu names remain searchable alongside translated names. Submenus sort
first, then actions, by their translated titles. Main and Apps retain their
existing order.

chapters.summary: Connecting, known networks, enterprise credentials, pairing and airplane mode
chapters.markdown:
# WiFi, Bluetooth and airplane mode

Open the bar icons or **System > Connectivity**. Opening a panel never changes
the selected backend or disconnects a device by itself.

## WiFi

The panel separates Connected, Known Networks and Other Networks. Choose an
available network to connect; password fields hide the password. Saved offline
networks remain visible without a fake signal percentage. Disconnect is on the
connected row; forgetting a saved network asks for confirmation.

The top section shows the network status, ping, the WiFi band, the IP address
and the gateway. The QR sharing control uses a supplied WiFi password and
keeps the generated image in memory. Enterprise credentials are not shared as
a personal-network QR code.

For enterprise networks, the panel supports PEAP/MSCHAPv2 and TTLS/PAP. Ask your
administrator for username, CA certificate and authentication-server domain;
do not disable certificate validation. Other authentication methods need
advanced provisioning. See [Network Backends](handbook:network-backends).

## Bluetooth

Toggle adapter power, scan, pair/connect, disconnect or forget devices. Connected,
known and newly discovered devices are grouped separately. Panel-started discovery
stops after 20 seconds or when the panel closes.

Pairing may need a PIN or confirmation agent. EITR's current desktop relies on
the Blueman agent for those dialogs; reconnecting an already-paired device does
not prove new-pairing support. Keep that agent until a PIN/confirmation pairing
has been tested. Clean-install pairing-agent coverage remains a known check.

## Airplane mode

Control Center > General blocks WiFi/Bluetooth using rfkill. Turning it off
restores only the radios it originally blocked. Hardware or externally applied
blocks are not silently overridden. Enable a radio individually if needed.

chapters.title: Remote Access
chapters.summary: Sunshine on Eitr, Moonlight on a Mac and Tailscale away from home
chapters.markdown:
# Remote access

Detailed Status opens a diagnostic terminal that stays open until you press Esc.

Use System > Connectivity > Remote Access. Hosting is off until you enable it.
This milestone controls your signed-in, awake Eitr desktop. Headless use, access
before login and wake on LAN are separate future work. Locked-session behaviour
has not been validated: stop sharing before locking when privacy matters.

## Sunshine on Eitr

Choose Share this PC > Set Up Sharing. Installation uses Eitr's signed native
Sunshine package, built from upstream sources by the release maintainer. There
is no AUR build on first click. Flatpak and AppImage lack KMS capture. Existing
Sunshine configuration and paired devices are kept; do not run another Sunshine
instance at the same time.

Read the full-control warning and type `yes` only if you accept KMS screen
capture and virtual keyboard, mouse and controller input. Setup saves the
original permissions privately in `/var/lib/eitr/remote-access`. It adds a uinput
udev rule, loads uinput at boot, grants the desktop user device access and gives
Sunshine `cap_sys_admin+p`. These are powerful permissions. Restore Sharing Setup
stops sharing and restores the saved files, capability and device ACL. If setup loaded uinput, undo unloads it too. If another application still uses it,
undo reports the failure and keeps the journal so you can close that application
and retry.

Start Sharing asks before giving remote devices control. The local web settings
open at `https://localhost:47990`. On first use, streaming stays blocked while you
set the password. Return to the terminal, confirm that it is set, then type `yes`
at the root helper’s confirmation to enable remote control. Accept the local self-signed certificate only
at that address. Set Sunshine's username and a strong password before pairing.
Open Settings returns here; Pair a Device opens the PIN page. Enter only the PIN
shown on your own Moonlight device. Keep automatic router configuration off;
Eitr enforces `upnp=off`. Do not configure router port forwarding.

TCP 47984, 47989 and 48010 and UDP 47998-48000 are permitted only from directly
connected private LAN subnets and `tailscale0`. TCP 47990 is restricted to this PC,
even when another firewall rule would permit it. LAN scopes are captured at each
start; stop and start sharing after changing networks. Use only trusted home
networks. Stop Sharing also disables start at login and closes streaming ports,
including established streams. Service failure closes them too; runtime openings
do not survive a reboot. Start at Login is optional and separately confirmed;
Turn Off Start at Login keeps manual sharing. Sharing Status shows service errors.

A Sunshine package update clears the executable’s capture capability. If sharing
then refuses to start, run Set Up Sharing again and confirm the capture grant;
the original undo record is retained.

## Moonlight on a Mac

Install Moonlight from [the Moonlight project](https://moonlight-stream.org/).
Keep Eitr and the Mac on the same home network for the first test. Add Eitr's LAN
address manually if discovery does not find it. Select the PC, read its PIN,
then use Pair a Device on Eitr. Select Desktop to control applications and games.
Sunshine settings select the captured display; verify each monitor separately.
Gaming > Moonlight and Connect to another PC install or open the Eitr client for
connecting in the opposite direction. Fresh installs include these apps; sharing stays off until explicitly enabled.

## Tailscale on both computers

Choose Access away from home > Set Up Away Access. After installing Tailscale,
the confirmed root helper enables and starts `tailscaled.service`, then makes
your desktop user its operator. Sign-in, Connect and Disconnect request administrator authorization so they also work when the operator has not been configured. Sign In
opens the URL printed by `tailscale login` in your browser. Connect brings the
PC online; Disconnect takes it offline without deleting sign-in credentials.
Connection Status shows this PC's Tailscale address, signed-out states and whether
active peers are Direct, Relayed or idle. Ping a Peer uses `tailscale ping` to
check a specific connection. Relay paths can increase latency and reduce quality.

Install [Tailscale on the Mac](https://tailscale.com/download/mac), sign in to the
same tailnet, and connect both computers. Add Eitr's Tailscale address in Moonlight;
use the same Sunshine pairing procedure. Tailnet access policy must allow the
streaming ports. The Sunshine web settings remain local to Eitr.

Restore Away Access Setup restores the previous operator and original service
startup/running state; it retains Tailscale account state and installed packages.
If the service was already active it stays active. Disconnect first if you want
to stop a connection. Failed installs or commands stay visible in the task terminal;
retry the failed step after resolving its error. No package removal is implicit.

## Validation still needed

Automated tests use mocks. With the owner, verify local Hyprland/NVIDIA capture,
keyboard, mouse, audio, controller, both monitors, lock behaviour, login startup,
then MacBook pairing and Tailscale direct/relay paths. Do not assume these hardware
behaviours have been verified by a green test suite.

chapters.title: Network Backends
chapters.summary: iwd, NetworkManager, reboot-only switching and enterprise configuration
chapters.markdown:
# Network backends

System > Connectivity > Network Backend selects iwd (the fresh-install default) or
NetworkManager with wpa_supplicant. Both use systemd-resolved for DNS. The
shared WiFi panel detects the running backend, not the saved next-boot choice.
The current connection is not restarted: the root-owned helper prepares files
and enables/disables boot services without `--now`, then asks whether to reboot.
Declining leaves the choice queued until your next reboot.

Saved WiFi profiles remain in each backend's own storage. They are not deleted
or automatically converted; reconnect on the first switch, and switching back
reuses the old profiles. Review custom static IP, VPN, bridge, networkd files or
other network managers before switching. Masked services, another active manager
or a custom resolver are refused rather than silently replaced. Original managed
files and service enable states are saved privately under
`/var/lib/eitr/network-backend`; Restore Original Network Configuration restores
them for the next boot, without stopping current networking.

The `eitr-desktop` package includes both backends and the root-owned helper
`/usr/lib/eitr/eitr-network`; install the package rather than copying the helper
by hand (see the distro README). A helper installed by hand earlier blocks the
package install until `distro/system/adopt-unowned-files.sh --apply` archives it.
Never elevate a helper from a user-writable path. Installing the helper does not
select a backend.

## Enterprise WiFi

The panel supports PEAP/MSCHAPv2 and TTLS/PAP, with username, optional anonymous
identity, password, authentication server domain and a PEM CA certificate path.
Ask the network administrator for these settings. Server certificate validation
is mandatory; EAP-TLS/client certificates, SIM/AKA and other advanced methods
still require external provisioning. Impala remains an optional fallback for
these configurations; do not remove it based on common-method support alone.

Credentials travel over process stdin and D-Bus, never command-line arguments.
NetworkManager stores its normal connection profile; iwd provisioning uses
PolicyKit authentication and a private root-owned `.8021x` profile with the CA
embedded. Existing enterprise profiles are not overwritten: forget the profile
explicitly before replacing it. Only root-owned, non-group/world-writable
helpers are accepted. No real backend switch, WiFi connection or enterprise
authentication is exercised by automated tests; validate both on spare hardware
or an isolated VM before describing them as hardware-tested.

chapters.title: Devices & Input
chapters.summary: Audio, microphone, brightness, displays, keyboard, battery and power profiles
chapters.markdown:
# Devices and input

Find these controls under **System > Devices & Input** or the corresponding bar
icons. The Control Center provides their everyday toggles and sliders too.

## Audio and microphone

Volume selects the default output and controls both master volume and playback
applications. Devices appear by readable name with a type icon; click the current
device to choose another, and use a device's pencil button to rename it on this
computer. Microphone selects the default input, gain and mute. The mic
panel's live level meter runs only while that panel is open; it writes no audio
to disk. Opening other settings does not start microphone monitoring.

Sliders adjust to 100%; an existing higher value is not changed until moved.
Changing your default audio device can affect a call: do it deliberately.
Media playback controls are separate from default device selection.

## Display and brightness

The Display panel lists active monitors. Click one to open its settings inside
its card; click it again to close them. The **Main** display holds the bar,
panels and notifications: turn on **Main display** in another monitor's settings
to move them there. If the main monitor disconnects, another display shows as
**Main** and takes the bar until it returns; your choice is kept.

A monitor's settings are its resolution, refresh rate, scale and, with more than
one monitor, its position beside another or mirroring. The main display stays
where it is and the others are placed around it, so its Position just says so;
a monitor can be placed beside any display except one already placed beside it.

Each setting is one row showing its current value; click it to see the choices.
Position, alignment, scale, mirroring and the main display apply and are saved at
once. A new **resolution or refresh rate** could leave a screen black, so for
those the panel asks **Keep these settings?** at its bottom edge: without
**Keep** within 15 seconds it goes back by itself, even if the panel is closed.
Settings are saved for this computer in `~/.config/hypr/displays.json`.

Any number of monitors can be arranged this way: place each one left of, right
of, above or below another, then align it with that monitor's top, middle or
bottom (left, center or right when stacked). The arrangement is remembered, so
when a monitor changes resolution or scale, the ones beside it move with it. A
choice that would make two monitors overlap is refused with a message. Every
connected monitor is given its exact place, so changing one never makes Hyprland
move the others.

**Edit layout by hand** opens `~/.config/hypr/local.lua` for what the panel does
not cover, such as rotated screens or workspaces pinned to a monitor. A new file
starts with commented examples (three monitors, portrait, stacked, mirroring,
a docked laptop); nothing changes until you uncomment one and run
`hyprctl reload`. Monitors set there take precedence over the panel; remove
them to manage those monitors here again.

Brightness prefers a usable native backlight; otherwise it tries an external
monitor through DDC. DDC availability depends on the monitor and permissions.
Night Light has a manual switch and an optional schedule with editable times.

## Keyboard

Add and remove layouts in Walker: System > Devices & Input > Keyboard. Add Layout
lists every language and variant (type to search); select a layout and press
Delete to remove it. Up to four layouts are supported, duplicates are rejected
and at least one layout must remain. **Alt + Shift** cycles them. With two or
more, the bar shows the active layout's code (such as US or BR); click it, or use
the Control Center, to switch. A keyboard layout is not the system language or locale.

The desktop starts with the keyboard you chose in the installer. Choosing US
gives both US and US International, so accents are one Alt + Shift away.

### Optional Caps Lock navigation

The optional keyd configuration in `distro/keyd/navigation.conf.example` makes
Caps Lock send Escape when tapped. Hold Caps Lock and press H/J/K/L for
Left/Down/Up/Right. Other keys keep their normal behavior.

To restore this preference after reinstalling, install that example as
`/etc/keyd/navigation.conf` and enable `keyd.service`. It applies to all keyboards,
including outside Hyprland, and is not enabled by default. To undo it, remove
that configuration and reload keyd; disable the service if no other mappings
use it. Keyboard language/layout selection remains separate.

## Laptop power and battery

Battery and power-profile controls appear only when a system battery exists,
not merely a wireless headset or mouse. Power Saver/Balanced/Performance need
power-profiles-daemon; unsupported profiles stay unavailable. Battery estimates
and health appear only when supplied by hardware.

Battery Charge Limit requires a supported firmware sysfs interface and typed
confirmation. Off allows charging to 100%. Do not assume every laptop supports it.

A notification warns at 10% battery and again, urgently, at 5%, once each time
the battery runs down. On laptops the installer also adds the audio firmware
most recent laptops need (`sof-firmware`) and, on Intel laptops, `thermald` to
manage heat.

These laptop features are **experimental** until early users confirm them on
real laptops: the keyboard backlight keys, and closing the lid while an external
monitor is connected, which turns the laptop screen off so the desktop moves to
the monitor (opening it brings the screen back). Without an external monitor,
closing the lid suspends as usual. Hibernation is not set up automatically.

chapters.markdown:
# Information, media and notifications

Notification cards show their local arrival date and time beneath the title,
in both popups and notification history. Times are kept only for this session.

## System > Information

**About** displays the EITR summary, including the installed EITR version, in a terminal. **Hardware** shows CPU, GPU,
RAM and storage for the drive backing `/`; other disks are not combined into
that total. Missing sensor/GPU telemetry is marked unavailable.

**AI Usage** detects installed/configured clients. Cached usage appears first;
refresh does not launch sign-in or conversations. It shows each account's
limits; percentages mean the part of a limit already used.

Every detected provider has its own section with its plan, limits and errors. Click a heading to fold or unfold only that section. All sections start expanded; folding is remembered on this machine. Long lists scroll within the screen.

**Weather** uses the default location and supports temporary city searches.
The override ends when the panel closes. Escape clears city search before
closing; temperature units follow the location, with an alternate unit alongside.

## Calendar and media

Click the clock/date for the calendar. It keeps six week rows and shows year
progress below the grid. Navigate with the previous/next buttons, Today, arrow
keys or T. Search Calendar from Walker if the bar is hidden.

Click the animated equalizer for cover/title/artist, previous/play/next and
seeking when supported. It hides without an eligible player and excludes
recognized meetings. The bars indicate playback, not captured audio.

## Notifications

**SUPER + N** or the bell opens the notification center. Notifications group by
application. The newest card fronts a stack; expand it to see older cards.
Dismiss one card or clear a group/all deliberately. Popups also stack by app,
showing the newest message over backing layers; hover pauses their expiry.

Notifications have a soft inward glow in the theme's accent colour; critical
ones glow in the theme's red instead, and low-priority ones are subdued with
no glow. Do Not Disturb suppresses popups
without deleting history. History stays in memory across config reloads, not
process restarts. No notification contents are saved as a log.

Every detected provider has its own section with its plan, limits and errors. Click a heading to fold or unfold only that section. All sections start expanded; folding is remembered on this machine. Long lists scroll within the screen.

Weather uses the default location and supports temporary city searches. The override ends when the panel closes. Escape clears city search before closing; temperature units follow the location, with an alternate unit alongside.
Calendar and media

Click the clock/date for the calendar. It keeps six week rows and shows year progress below the grid. Navigate with the previous/next buttons, Today, arrow keys or T. Search Calendar from Walker if the bar is hidden.

Click the animated equalizer for cover/title/artist, previous/play/next and seeking when supported. It hides without an eligible player and excludes recognized meetings. The bars indicate playback, not captured audio.
Notifications

SUPER + N or the bell opens the notification center. Notifications group by application. The newest card fronts a stack; expand it to see older cards. Dismiss one card or clear a group/all deliberately. Popups also stack by app, showing the newest message over backing layers; hover pauses their expiry.

Notifications have a soft inward glow in the theme's accent colour; critical ones glow in the theme's red instead, and low-priority ones are subdued with no glow. Do Not Disturb suppresses popups without deleting history. History stays in memory across config reloads, not process restarts. No notification contents are saved as a log.

# Security and locking

**SUPER + M** locks now. Click the Idle Lock icon on the left of the bar (after
AI Usage) to turn automatic idle locking on or off; its tooltip shows which.
When on, the screen locks after 15 minutes idle, turns off after 30 and the
computer sleeps after 60. The Control Center has the same Idle Lock toggle and
a Lock button.

## Password and alternative authentication

**System > Security > Update Password** changes your account password.
Fingerprint and FIDO2 have their own enrollment/enable workflows. A FIDO2
security key is a physical security device, not a laptop fingerprint reader.
Enroll first, then enable authentication. The helper backs up PAM settings;
keep a working password and a way to reach a TTY.

Return to Password Authentication restores password-only behavior. These
changes affect supported lockscreen/login/sudo PAM services; hardware support
and installed helpers are required. Fingerprint authentication may delay a
password prompt briefly. Reading this page does not modify PAM.

## Firewall

New installations start with the firewall on. It refuses incoming connections
except replies to something your computer started, local name discovery, and the
sharing apps Eitr installs: KDE Connect (ports 1714-1764) and LocalSend (53317).
Virtual machines and containers on your computer still reach it, and outgoing
traffic is never filtered. When SSH is enabled, SSH stays reachable too.

**System > Security > Firewall** shows whether it is on and switches it after you
confirm. Computers set up before the firewall existed start with it off. To let
another app accept connections, add a file to `/etc/eitr/firewall.d/`, for
example `game.nft` containing:

```
add rule inet eitr_firewall input udp dport 27015 accept
```

then turn the firewall off and on again.

## Disk encryption and TPM

Disk encryption is an installer choice. TPM Disk Unlock can add a TPM2 slot to
a supported existing LUKS2 root; it is not automatically enrolled by the
installer. Keep a passphrase/recovery key offline. Never save it in screenshots
or repository files. Firmware/Secure Boot changes can require the passphrase
at the next boot.

Read [Recovery & Snapshots](handbook:recovery) before changing authentication or
TPM setup. [Secure Boot](handbook:secure-boot) is an advanced, manual process:
EITR does not enroll firmware keys or sign boot files for you. A mistake can
prevent booting or even reaching firmware setup on some hardware.

chapters.markdown:
# Updates, cleanup and recovery

The terminal names each update check and snapshot stage while it runs. If everything is up to date, the message stays visible for three seconds before the terminal closes.

Open **System > Maintenance**. Review terminal output and keep independent
backups before system changes. Snapshot protection is not an off-disk backup.

System Update first checks official packages with checkupdates in a separate temporary database, AUR packages (including development packages), and user Flatpaks. When all checks confirm no updates, it exits without snapshots, upgrades or a restart prompt. If a check fails or a tool is missing, the normal update workflow continues.

## Update

**Update > System Update** is the normal complete package-update workflow.
On a configured fresh EITR distro, it verifies snapshot support and creates
pre/post snapshots with boot archives. If protection fails, no upgrade begins.
An existing Arch desktop without the distro policy does not require this setup
just to update. System Update also updates apps installed from Flatpak, such as
GeForce NOW; a Flatpak failure is reported without undoing the system update.

Before upgrading, System Update (and the Pacman updates under Advanced) checks
Arch Linux's news for posts since your last upgrade. Arch uses them to announce
upgrades that need a manual step. When there is news, it shows the titles and
links and asks **Continue the update? [y/N]**: Enter cancels before anything
changes, so you can read the post first. Without news, or without internet, it
just continues.

**Update > Update Channel** lists both channels with yours marked; choosing the
other asks for your password in a terminal and switches. It chooses where Eitr's
own updates come from. Stable,
the default, gets them once they have been tried. Testing gets new builds as
soon as they are published, to try changes early; everything else still comes
from Arch. Switching back to stable keeps a newer Eitr version until stable
catches up. From a terminal: `eitr channel` shows it, `eitr channel testing` or
`eitr channel stable` switches.

If an update leaves the computer unable to start, the **boot guard** undoes it:
when two starts in a row after an update never reach the login screen, the next
start restores the system and boot files from just before the update and
restarts. Your home folder is not touched, and the next login tells you what
happened. It works on computers installed with the Eitr installer; see
[Recovery & Snapshots](handbook:recovery) for the details.

**Home folder snapshots** keep earlier versions of your own files: turn them on
in **System > Maintenance > Snapshots > Home Folder Snapshots**. They are taken
every hour for a day and every day for a week, and the oldest go when the disk
gets full; caches, Downloads, VM disks and games are left out. To get a file
back, choose **Restore a File or Folder**, type its path and pick a time. The
old version appears next to the current one, so nothing is replaced.

**Update > Advanced** offers **Pacman + Yay**, **Pacman**, and **Yay (AUR)**.
These intentionally do not create automatic snapshots. Direct pacman/yay
commands also bypass the protected workflow. Flatpaks, development runtimes and
separate home data are not covered by root snapshots.

Avoid partial Arch upgrades. Read package prompts rather than accepting an
unexpected removal blindly. Successful update tasks close; failures remain
visible so you can troubleshoot rather than lose their output.

After a successful update, a notification asks to finish it when needed:
**Restart now** after kernel, firmware, microcode, systemd, glibc, graphics
driver or disk-encryption updates, or **Log out now** after desktop updates
such as EITR, Hyprland, Quickshell, Walker or PipeWire. **Later** keeps working;
the new versions take effect at the next restart or login.

## Cleanup and snapshots

Cleanup runs its maintenance workflow and keeps the report open for reading.
Review what it proposes; do not treat every orphan package as unused.
Snapshots offers the existing Snapper status/configuration workflows. Read
[Recovery & Snapshots](handbook:recovery) for supported layouts and bootloader limits.

## Factory reset

Only a supported distro install with its first-login restore point can reset.
That private baseline is separate from ordinary Snapper lists and cleanup.
Root can still delete it, and disk failure can destroy it. Two separate warnings
and a typed confirmation are required. Read [Factory Reset](handbook:factory-reset)
for exactly what Erase Everything and Keep My Files preserve.

## Power

Main > Power and Control Center > General (behind **Power…**) expose Lock,
Logout, Suspend, Reboot and Shutdown. Save work first. These are actions, not simulated demonstrations.

chapters.summary: Btrfs, Snapper, boot backups, authentication recovery and TPM
chapters.markdown:
# Eitr recovery snapshots

Snapshots are recovery points, **not off-machine backups**. A failed disk can
destroy the system and its snapshots together. Keep independent backups.

Eitr currently supports Snapper on a Btrfs root with `/usr`, `/etc` and
`/var/lib/pacman` in the same root subvolume. `/home` may be separate: it is not
covered by a root snapshot. Unsupported layouts fail closed before upgrades.
`install.sh` does not format disks or rearrange existing subvolumes; only the
ISO's `eitr-guided-install` erases the disk you confirm, creating this layout
(see the README's Guided install section).

## Before updates

The installer enables `/etc/eitr/system-update-policy.conf`. Before
System → Maintenance → Update → System Update upgrades official and AUR packages, it:

1. Verifies the supported layout and Snapper root configuration.
2. Archives `/boot` and `/efi` only when they are separate mounts (a `/boot`
   directory inside the Btrfs root is already in the root snapshot). Archives
   are stored under `/var/lib/eitr/boot-backups/<snapshot-number>/` with
   root-only access.
3. Creates a pre-upgrade root snapshot.
4. Aborts the upgrade if boot backup or snapshot creation fails.

When the upgrade finishes, fails or is declined, the workflow creates the
corresponding post snapshot; its description records the outcome ("after
package upgrade", "after failed package upgrade"). If the workflow was killed
before that, the next System Update first closes the leftover pre snapshot
with an "after interrupted package upgrade" post snapshot. A failed upgrade
retains its pre snapshot and boot archives either way.
Updates to Flatpaks, SDKMAN/NVM runtimes and files on separate home subvolumes are
not protected by these snapshots. Advanced updates and direct pacman/yay commands
intentionally do not create automatic snapshots. Older Eitr snapshot hooks, if
manually installed, must be removed to adopt this policy.

New Snapper configurations keep up to 10 ordinary and 5 important numbered
snapshots through the cleanup timer. Existing policies are preserved. Boot
archives are pruned on each System Update to the newest 10, matching the
default snapshot limit; an archive may outlive its snapshot if Snapper removes
it first, so check the snapshot exists before restoring one. A full disk
prevents updates rather than skipping protection.

## Boot guard

After a successful System Update on Eitr's guided-install layout, the boot guard
keeps that update's "before" snapshot ready (`/var/lib/eitr/boot-guard.json`).
`eitr-boot-guard.service` counts each start early in boot, and
`eitr-boot-guard-healthy.service` counts a start as healthy once the login screen
has stayed up for 45 seconds, which disarms the guard.

When two starts in a row after the update never reach that point, the third start
restores automatically, using the factory reset's tested steps:

1. The snapshot's boot files (`/var/lib/eitr/boot-backups/<number>/boot.tar`) are
   copied to the EFI partition, after keeping today's boot files to put back.
2. The failed root subvolume is renamed `@eitr-guard-failed`, a writable copy of
   the snapshot becomes `@`, and Snapper's `.snapshots` store moves into it.
3. The computer restarts into the restored system. If any step fails, the
   subvolumes and boot files are put back as they were and nothing restarts.

The restored system deletes `@eitr-guard-failed` once it reaches the login
screen, and the next login shows a notification. Home folders are not touched.
The guard cannot help when the kernel itself does not start; boot the update's
snapshot from the boot menu instead (below). Other disk layouts are never armed.

## Authentication changes

Security → Enable Fingerprint/FIDO2 backs up `/etc/pam.d/hyprlock`, `sddm` and
`sudo` under `/var/lib/eitr/pam-backups/<timestamp>/` before editing them, and
restores all three if any write fails. Fingerprint is added to all three, so
"password only" applies to the lockscreen too; pam_fprintd may delay the
password prompt for up to 10 seconds. To return to an earlier policy from a working root
shell or TTY:

```sh
sudo ls /var/lib/eitr/pam-backups
sudo /usr/lib/eitr/eitr-system auth-restore <timestamp>
# Without the eitr-desktop package, the helper is /usr/local/lib/eitr/eitr-system.
```

## TPM disk unlock

Security → TPM Disk Unlock can add a TPM2 key slot to a LUKS2 root so the disk
unlocks at boot without typing the passphrase. Nothing here runs from the
installer. The root helper (`luks-tpm-check`, `luks-recovery-key`,
`luks-tpm-enroll`, `luks-tpm-remove`) refuses unless the device is LUKS2, a TPM2
device is listed by `systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=list`, and a passphrase
or recovery slot already exists. It only **adds** a slot; the passphrase stays.

- **Recovery key first.** The Walker flow offers
  `systemd-cryptenroll --recovery-key`; the key is printed once to the terminal
  and never stored. Write it down offline. It works at the normal passphrase prompt.
- **PCR choice.** Eitr binds to PCR 7 (Secure Boot state and keys). Firmware
  updates rarely change it, while a Secure Boot key change does. PCR 7 only
  protects much when Secure Boot is enabled with your own keys (see
  [SECURE-BOOT.md](handbook:secure-boot)); otherwise anyone can boot this machine
  with an edited kernel command line and get an unlocked disk. For stronger
  protection, enroll manually with a PIN:
  `sudo systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7 --tpm2-with-pin=yes <device>`.
- **Initramfs.** The busybox `encrypt` hook cannot use TPM2 tokens, so
  enrollment refuses while it is configured. Switching to `systemd` and
  `sd-encrypt` in `HOOKS` (with `rd.luks.name=<LUKS-UUID>=root` replacing
  `cryptdevice=` on the kernel command line, or `/etc/crypttab.initramfs`) is a
  boot-critical change Eitr leaves to you. Make it, run `sudo mkinitcpio -P`,
  update the boot entry, and confirm one passphrase boot works **before**
  enrolling the TPM.

If the TPM stops unlocking (firmware or Secure Boot change, TPM reset), the
passphrase prompt appears as before. Enter it, then remove and re-enroll. To
roll back completely, use Remove TPM Unlock, or from any working shell:

```sh
sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/<luks-partition>            # list slots
sudo systemd-cryptenroll --wipe-slot=tpm2 /dev/<luks-partition>
```

## Factory reset

Computers installed with the Eitr ISO also keep a read-only first-login restore
point outside Snapper. Walker → System → Maintenance → Factory Reset returns to it, with or
without the home folder files; see [FACTORY-RESET.md](handbook:factory-reset).

## Inspect recovery points

Use Walker → System → Maintenance → Snapshots, or run these read-only checks:

```sh
sudo snapper -c root list
findmnt -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE / /boot /efi
sudo du -sh /var/lib/eitr/boot-backups
```

If the desktop fails but the system still boots, switch to a text console or use
an SSH connection you configured yourself. If it does not boot, use the official
Arch installer ISO and mount the system's Btrfs filesystem. Identify the correct
disk, encryption mapping, root subvolume, snapshot number and EFI mount before
making any changes. Do not copy commands from another machine blindly.

## Home folder snapshots

Off by default. **System > Maintenance > Snapshots > Home Folder Snapshots**
turns them on (it asks first, and turning them off deletes them). Snapper's
`home` configuration then keeps a snapshot of `/home` every hour for a day and
one a day for a week, deleting the oldest when free space falls below 20%.

Caches, `~/Downloads`, VM disk folders (`~/.local/share/libvirt/images`,
GNOME Boxes, `~/VirtualBox VMs`) and the Steam library are left out: at the
next start, before anyone logs in, `eitr-home-exclusions.service` turns them into
nested Btrfs subvolumes, which home snapshots do not include. Their files are
kept (reflinked, so the move takes no extra space). The factory reset's Keep My
Files carries these subvolumes into the restored home: hidden ones into the
"Settings before reset" folder, caches are dropped. If one cannot be moved, the
previous home is kept for review instead of deleted.

**Snapshots > Restore a File or Folder** (or `eitr restore PATH`) lists the
snapshots that have the path and copies the chosen version beside the current
one as `NAME (restored DATE)`, or back in place when it was deleted. Nothing is
ever overwritten.

## What each update changed

Before rolling back, check what you would undo. **System > Maintenance >
Snapshots > What Each Update Changed** (or `eitr snapshots changes`) lists every
update's before/after pair with counts of upgraded, downgraded, installed and
removed packages. `eitr snapshots changes <before number>` lists every package of
one update with its old and new version. It compares the package databases kept
inside the two snapshots; an update that has no after snapshot yet is compared
with the running system.

## Boot an older snapshot

With GRUB or Limine, the boot menu can list read-only Snapper snapshots, so a
broken update can be inspected and rolled back without live media. The
installer offers this only after you type `yes`; on an existing installation run
`bash distro/bootloader/setup.sh` (`--check` only reports). Check the result with
Walker → System → Maintenance → Snapshots → Bootable Snapshot Status, or
`sudo /usr/lib/eitr/eitr-system snapshots-boot-status`.

| Boot loader | Integration | Packages (`distro/bootloader/`) |
|---|---|---|
| GRUB | `grub-btrfsd.service` rebuilds the "Arch Linux snapshots" submenu whenever Snapper adds or removes a snapshot | `grub-btrfs`, `inotify-tools` (official) |
| Limine | `limine-snapper-sync.service` adds snapshot entries to `limine.conf` | `limine-snapper-sync`, `limine-mkinitcpio-hook` (AUR) |
| systemd-boot | **Not supported.** It only loads kernels from the EFI/XBOOTLDR partition and cannot open Btrfs snapshots | Use the live-media procedure below |

Detection reads the GRUB, Limine and systemd-boot files under `/boot`, `/efi`
and `/boot/efi`. If more than one loader is configured (for example leftover
systemd-boot files next to GRUB), setup refuses rather than guessing; remove the
stale files or configure entries manually. Setup copies the current
`grub.cfg`/`limine.conf` to `/var/lib/eitr/boot-config-backups/<timestamp>/`
first, and enables the service for the next boot:

- **GRUB:** setup runs `grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg` once. If `/boot`
  is a separate partition, snapshot entries boot the *current* kernel; after a
  kernel update, restore the matching boot archive (see below) as well.
- **Limine:** `limine-snapper-sync` manages entries created by
  `limine-entry-tool` (from `limine-mkinitcpio-hook`) and keeps copies of each
  snapshot's kernel on the EFI partition, so that partition needs room (upstream
  recommends 4 GiB). Review `/etc/default/limine` (`SNAPPER_CONFIG_NAME="root"`,
  `ESP_PATH` if not detected), run `sudo limine-update`, check the menu, then
  `sudo systemctl start limine-snapper-sync.service`. Eitr does not run
  `limine-update` for you because it rewrites the boot menu.

To undo, disable the service and copy the backup back, for example
`sudo systemctl disable grub-btrfsd.service` and
`sudo cp /var/lib/eitr/boot-config-backups/<timestamp>/grub.cfg /boot/grub/grub.cfg`.

### Read-only snapshots

Snapper snapshots are read-only. A snapshot booted as-is cannot write `/var`, so
SDDM and other services may fail; log in on a text console (Ctrl+Alt+F3) if the
graphical login does not start. An initramfs overlay makes the booted snapshot
writable in RAM (changes vanish at reboot). Eitr does not edit `HOOKS`; add it
yourself, then regenerate, and note that only snapshots created afterwards
contain the hook:

- GRUB: append `grub-btrfs-overlayfs` to `HOOKS=(...)` in `/etc/mkinitcpio.conf`,
  then `sudo mkinitcpio -P`.
- Limine: add `btrfs-overlayfs` after `filesystems` (or `sd-btrfs-overlayfs`
  with the systemd hooks), then `sudo limine-update`.

### Roll back for good

1. Pick the newest "before package upgrade" snapshot in the boot menu's
   snapshot list and confirm the system works there.
2. **Limine:** run `sudo limine-snapper-restore` and choose the snapshot. It
   restores with the configured `RESTORE_METHOD` and adds a backup entry for the
   replaced system, so the restore itself can be reverted from the boot menu.
3. **GRUB:** `snapper rollback` only works when the root is mounted through the
   Btrfs default subvolume. Arch layouts usually boot `rootflags=subvol=@`
   (check `findmnt -no OPTIONS /` and `/etc/fstab`), so rollback would have no
   effect. Replace the root subvolume from live media after inspecting the
   top-level filesystem's subvolume list. The following example is **only** for
   Eitr's guided-install layout, where Snapper created the nested
   `@/.snapshots` subvolume; other layouts need their actual paths:

   ```sh
   sudo mount -o subvolid=5 /dev/<root-or-mapper> /mnt
   sudo mv /mnt/@ /mnt/@.broken
   sudo btrfs subvolume snapshot /mnt/@.broken/.snapshots/<number>/snapshot /mnt/@
   # A Btrfs snapshot does not include nested subvolumes. Keep the original
   # Snapper store in the restored root instead of deleting it with @.broken.
   sudo rmdir /mnt/@/.snapshots
   sudo mv /mnt/@.broken/.snapshots /mnt/@/.snapshots
   ```

   If any command fails, stop and inspect; do not delete the preserved root.
   Verify the snapshot store is present under the restored root, and review
   its fstab before proceeding. Restore the matching
   `/var/lib/eitr/boot-backups/<number>/` archive if `/boot`
   is separate, reboot into the normal entry, run
   `sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg`, and delete `@.broken` with
   `sudo btrfs subvolume delete` only after the restored system is verified.

## Restore safely from live media

1. Back up any newer files you need. Mount the Btrfs top-level filesystem and
   inspect its subvolume list; locate the selected snapshot's `snapshot`
   subvolume. Paths depend on where `.snapshots` is mounted.
2. Preserve the failed root subvolume by renaming it. Create a **writable Btrfs
   snapshot** of the selected recovery snapshot at the original root-subvolume
   path, matching the installed bootloader's rootflags and fstab.

   matching boot archives if kernel/initramfs/bootloader files changed. Archives
   must match the chosen root snapshot; never mix a newer kernel with older modules.
4. Review fstab and bootloader configuration, then regenerate initramfs or repair
   boot entries from `arch-chroot` as needed for that machine. Reboot only after
   the root and boot files agree.

blocks: Eitr recovery snapshots
Snapshots are recovery points, not off-machine backups. A failed disk can destroy the system and its snapshots together. Keep independent backups.

Eitr currently supports Snapper on a Btrfs root with /usr, /etc and /var/lib/pacman in the same root subvolume. /home may be separate: it is not covered by a root snapshot. Unsupported layouts fail closed before upgrades. install.sh does not format disks or rearrange existing subvolumes; only the ISO's eitr-guided-install erases the disk you confirm, creating this layout (see the README's Guided install section).
Before updates
The installer enables /etc/eitr/system-update-policy.conf. Before System → Maintenance → Update → System Update upgrades official and AUR packages, it:

1. Verifies the supported layout and Snapper root configuration.
  2. Archives /boot and /efi only when they are separate mounts (a /boot directory inside the Btrfs root is already in the root snapshot). Archives are stored under /var/lib/eitr/boot-backups/<snapshot-number>/ with root-only access.
  3. Creates a pre-upgrade root snapshot.
  4. Aborts the upgrade if boot backup or snapshot creation fails.

When the upgrade finishes, fails or is declined, the workflow creates the corresponding post snapshot; its description records the outcome ("after package upgrade", "after failed package upgrade"). If the workflow was killed before that, the next System Update first closes the leftover pre snapshot with an "after interrupted package upgrade" post snapshot. A failed upgrade retains its pre snapshot and boot archives either way. Updates to Flatpaks, SDKMAN/NVM runtimes and files on separate home subvolumes are not protected by these snapshots. Advanced updates and direct pacman/yay commands intentionally do not create automatic snapshots. Older Eitr snapshot hooks, if manually installed, must be removed to adopt this policy.

New Snapper configurations keep up to 10 ordinary and 5 important numbered snapshots through the cleanup timer. Existing policies are preserved. Boot archives are pruned on each System Update to the newest 10, matching the default snapshot limit; an archive may outlive its snapshot if Snapper removes it first, so check the snapshot exists before restoring one. A full disk prevents updates rather than skipping protection.
Boot guard

After a successful System Update on Eitr's guided-install layout, the boot guard keeps that update's "before" snapshot ready (/var/lib/eitr/boot-guard.json). eitr-boot-guard.service counts each start early in boot, and eitr-boot-guard-healthy.service counts a start as healthy once the login screen has stayed up for 45 seconds, which disarms the guard.
When two starts in a row after the update never reach that point, the third start restores automatically, using the factory reset's tested steps:

1. The snapshot's boot files (/var/lib/eitr/boot-backups/<number>/boot.tar) are copied to the EFI partition, after keeping today's boot files to put back.
  2. The failed root subvolume is renamed @eitr-guard-failed, a writable copy of the snapshot becomes @, and Snapper's .snapshots store moves into it.
  3. The computer restarts into the restored system. If any step fails, the subvolumes and boot files are put back as they were and nothing restarts.

The restored system deletes @eitr-guard-failed once it reaches the login screen, and the next login shows a notification. Home folders are not touched. The guard cannot help when the kernel itself does not start; boot the update's snapshot from the boot menu instead (below). Other disk layouts are never armed.
Authentication changes

Security → Enable Fingerprint/FIDO2 backs up /etc/pam.d/hyprlock, sddm and sudo under /var/lib/eitr/pam-backups/<timestamp>/ before editing them, and restores all three if any write fails. Fingerprint is added to all three, so "password only" applies to the lockscreen too; pam_fprintd may delay the password prompt for up to 10 seconds. To return to an earlier policy from a working root shell or TTY:

sudo ls /var/lib/eitr/pam-backups
sudo /usr/lib/eitr/eitr-system auth-restore <timestamp>
# Without the eitr-desktop package, the helper is /usr/local/lib/eitr/eitr-system.
TPM disk unlock

Security → TPM Disk Unlock can add a TPM2 key slot to a LUKS2 root so the disk unlocks at boot without typing the passphrase. Nothing here runs from the installer. The root helper (luks-tpm-check, luks-recovery-key, luks-tpm-enroll, luks-tpm-remove) refuses unless the device is LUKS2, a TPM2 device is listed by systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=list, and a passphrase or recovery slot already exists. It only adds a slot; the passphrase stays.

• Recovery key first. The Walker flow offers systemd-cryptenroll --recovery-key; the key is printed once to the terminal and never stored. Write it down offline. It works at the normal passphrase prompt.
  • PCR choice. Eitr binds to PCR 7 (Secure Boot state and keys). Firmware updates rarely change it, while a Secure Boot key change does. PCR 7 only protects much when Secure Boot is enabled with your own keys (see SECURE-BOOT.md); otherwise anyone can boot this machine with an edited kernel command line and get an unlocked disk. For stronger protection, enroll manually with a PIN: sudo systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7 --tpm2-with-pin=yes <device>.
  • Initramfs. The busybox encrypt hook cannot use TPM2 tokens, so enrollment refuses while it is configured. Switching to systemd and sd-encrypt in HOOKS (with rd.luks.name=<LUKS-UUID>=root replacing cryptdevice= on the kernel command line, or /etc/crypttab.initramfs) is a boot-critical change Eitr leaves to you. Make it, run sudo mkinitcpio -P, update the boot entry, and confirm one passphrase boot works before enrolling the TPM.

If the TPM stops unlocking (firmware or Secure Boot change, TPM reset), the passphrase prompt appears as before. Enter it, then remove and re-enroll. To roll back completely, use Remove TPM Unlock, or from any working shell:

sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/<luks-partition>            # list slots
sudo systemd-cryptenroll --wipe-slot=tpm2 /dev/<luks-partition>

Computers installed with the Eitr ISO also keep a read-only first-login restore point outside Snapper. Walker → System → Maintenance → Factory Reset returns to it, with or without the home folder files; see FACTORY-RESET.md.

Use Walker → System → Maintenance → Snapshots, or run these read-only checks:

sudo snapper -c root list
findmnt -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE / /boot /efi
sudo du -sh /var/lib/eitr/boot-backups

Home folder snapshots

Off by default. System > Maintenance > Snapshots > Home Folder Snapshots turns them on (it asks first, and turning them off deletes them). Snapper's home configuration then keeps a snapshot of /home every hour for a day and one a day for a week, deleting the oldest when free space falls below 20%.

Caches, ~/Downloads, VM disk folders (~/.local/share/libvirt/images, GNOME Boxes, ~/VirtualBox VMs) and the Steam library are left out: at the next start, before anyone logs in, eitr-home-exclusions.service turns them into nested Btrfs subvolumes, which home snapshots do not include.
