Snapshots > Restore a File or Folder (or eitr restore PATH) lists the snapshots that have the path and copies the chosen version beside the current one as NAME (restored DATE), or back in place when it was deleted. Nothing is ever overwritten.
What each update changed

Before rolling back, check what you would undo. System > Maintenance > Snapshots > What Each Update Changed (or eitr snapshots changes) lists every update's before/after pair with counts of upgraded, downgraded, installed and removed packages. eitr snapshots changes <before number> lists every package of one update with its old and new version. It compares the package databases kept inside the two snapshots; an update that has no after snapshot yet is compared with the running system.
Boot an older snapshot

With GRUB or Limine, the boot menu can list read-only Snapper snapshots, so a broken update can be inspected and rolled back without live media. The installer offers this only after you type yes; on an existing installation run bash distro/bootloader/setup.sh (--check only reports). Check the result with Walker → System → Maintenance → Snapshots → Bootable Snapshot Status, or sudo /usr/lib/eitr/eitr-system snapshots-boot-status.

Boot loader Integration Packages (distro/bootloader/)
GRUB grub-btrfsd.service rebuilds the "Arch Linux snapshots" submenu whenever Snapper adds or removes a snapshot grub-btrfs, inotify-tools (official)
Limine limine-snapper-sync.service adds snapshot entries to limine.conf limine-snapper-sync, limine-mkinitcpio-hook (AUR)
systemd-boot Not supported. It only loads kernels from the EFI/XBOOTLDR partition and cannot open Btrfs snapshots Use the live-media procedure below

Detection reads the GRUB, Limine and systemd-boot files under /boot, /efi and /boot/efi. If more than one loader is configured (for example leftover systemd-boot files next to GRUB), setup refuses rather than guessing; remove the stale files or configure entries manually. Setup copies the current grub.cfg/limine.conf to /var/lib/eitr/boot-config-backups/<timestamp>/ first, and enables the service for the next boot:

• GRUB: setup runs grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg once. If /boot is a separate partition, snapshot entries boot the current kernel; after a kernel update, restore the matching boot archive (see below) as well.
  • Limine: limine-snapper-sync manages entries created by limine-entry-tool (from limine-mkinitcpio-hook) and keeps copies of each snapshot's kernel on the EFI partition, so that partition needs room (upstream recommends 4 GiB). Review /etc/default/limine (SNAPPER_CONFIG_NAME="root", ESP_PATH if not detected), run sudo limine-update, check the menu, then sudo systemctl start limine-snapper-sync.service. Eitr does not run limine-update for you because it rewrites the boot menu.
To undo, disable the service and copy the backup back, for example sudo systemctl disable grub-btrfsd.service and sudo cp /var/lib/eitr/boot-config-backups/<timestamp>/grub.cfg /boot/grub/grub.cfg.
Read-only snapshots

Snapper snapshots are read-only. A snapshot booted as-is cannot write /var, so SDDM and other services may fail; log in on a text console (Ctrl+Alt+F3) if the graphical login does not start. An initramfs overlay makes the booted snapshot writable in RAM (changes vanish at reboot). Eitr does not edit HOOKS; add it yourself, then regenerate, and note that only snapshots created afterwards contain the hook:

• GRUB: append grub-btrfs-overlayfs to HOOKS=(...) in /etc/mkinitcpio.conf, then sudo mkinitcpio -P.
  • Limine: add btrfs-overlayfs after filesystems (or sd-btrfs-overlayfs with the systemd hooks), then sudo limine-update.
Roll back for good

1. Pick the newest "before package upgrade" snapshot in the boot menu's snapshot list and confirm the system works there.
  2. Limine: run sudo limine-snapper-restore and choose the snapshot. It restores with the configured RESTORE_METHOD and adds a backup entry for the replaced system, so the restore itself can be reverted from the boot menu.
  3. GRUB: snapper rollback only works when the root is mounted through the Btrfs default subvolume. Arch layouts usually boot rootflags=subvol=@ (check findmnt -no OPTIONS / and /etc/fstab), so rollback would have no effect. Replace the root subvolume from live media after inspecting the top-level filesystem's subvolume list. The following example is only for Eitr's guided-install layout, where Snapper created the nested @/.snapshots subvolume; other layouts need their actual paths:

sudo mount -o subvolid=5 /dev/<root-or-mapper> /mnt
sudo mv /mnt/@ /mnt/@.broken
sudo btrfs subvolume snapshot /mnt/@.broken/.snapshots/<number>/snapshot /mnt/@
# A Btrfs snapshot does not include nested subvolumes. Keep the original
# Snapper store in the restored root instead of deleting it with @.broken.
sudo rmdir /mnt/@/.snapshots
sudo mv /mnt/@.broken/.snapshots /mnt/@/.snapshots

If any command fails, stop and inspect; do not delete the preserved root. Verify the snapshot store is present under the restored root, and review its fstab before proceeding. Restore the matching /var/lib/eitr/boot-backups/<number>/ archive if /boot is separate, reboot into the normal entry, run sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg, and delete @.broken with sudo btrfs subvolume delete only after the restored system is verified.
Restore safely from live media

1. Back up any newer files you need. Mount the Btrfs top-level filesystem and inspect its subvolume list; locate the selected snapshot's snapshot subvolume. Paths depend on where .snapshots is mounted.
  2. Preserve the failed root subvolume by renaming it. Create a writable Btrfs snapshot of the selected recovery snapshot at the original root-subvolume path, matching the installed bootloader's rootflags and fstab.
  3. Mount that restored root and its actual boot/EFI partitions. Restore the matching boot archives if kernel/initramfs/bootloader files changed. Archives must match the chosen root snapshot; never mix a newer kernel with older modules.
  4. Review fstab and bootloader configuration, then regenerate initramfs or repair boot entries from arch-chroot as needed for that machine. Reboot only after the root and boot files agree.

This is a layout-aware manual recovery procedure, not a verified one-click rollback implementation. Snapper's rollback command alone is not sufficient for arbitrary Arch subvolume/bootloader layouts. The GRUB and Limine snapshot entries above still need validation on real hardware before claiming automatic recovery.

# Factory reset

Computers installed with the Eitr ISO can return to the state of their first
login from Walker → System → Maintenance → Factory Reset. The reset is local: it restores a
read-only copy saved on the same disk. It is not a backup and not secure
erasure; a failed disk loses the computer and its restore point together.

## The restore point

The guided installer's last step runs `eitr-factory-reset capture`, which saves
the finished installation under the top-level Btrfs subvolume `@eitr-factory`:

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `root` | read-only snapshot of `@` (system, accounts, settings) |
| `home` | read-only snapshot of `@home` (the seeded user folders) |
| `boot.tar` | the EFI partition's files: Limine, its menu, kernel and initramfs |
| `manifest.json` | creation time, filesystem and EFI partition UUIDs, accounts, `boot.tar` SHA-256 |

`@eitr-factory` itself is then made read-only. It lives beside `@`, not in
`@/.snapshots`, so Snapper never lists it or cleans it up, and Walker offers no
way to delete it. Root can still delete it, and formatting or disk failure
destroys it. Its snapshots share data with the running system, so it costs
little space at first and grows as updates replace the original files.

`capture` refuses to replace an existing restore point. Installations made
without the ISO have none, and Factory Reset reports that.

## The two resets

**Erase Everything** returns the computer to its first login: apps installed
since, changed settings, accounts added later and every file in the home
folders are gone.

**Keep My Files** restores the system, apps and settings, and keeps the home
folders. For each account in the restore point, its current hidden entries
(`~/.config`, `~/.local`, `~/.ssh`, browser profiles and so on) move into a
visible folder named `Settings before reset <date time>` in that home folder,
then the restore point's hidden entries are copied back. Nothing in a home
folder is deleted. Accounts added after installation are removed with the
system, but their home folders stay under `/home`.

Both resets keep the disk encryption passphrase (the LUKS header is never
touched) and the current password of every account that the restore point
also has. A TPM unlock slot stays in the LUKS header, but the restored
initramfs asks for the passphrase until TPM unlock is set up again. Logs
(`@log`) and the package cache (`@pkg`) are kept.

## Confirmation

Walker's action shows two separate warnings in a terminal:

1. What the chosen reset removes and keeps. Only `y` or `yes` continues; Enter
   cancels.
2. Which computer is reset, that it restarts immediately and that unsaved work
   is lost. Typing `RESET MY COMPUTER` exactly is required.

The root-owned helper (`/usr/lib/eitr/eitr-factory-reset`) checks the typed
phrase again and validates before changing anything:

- `/` is subvolume `@` and `/home` is `@home` on one Btrfs filesystem, and
  `/boot` is the FAT EFI partition.
- The restore point and its snapshots are still read-only, its manifest names
  this filesystem and EFI partition, and `boot.tar` matches its SHA-256.
- Secure Boot is off: restored boot files are not signed with enrolled keys.
- No earlier reset is still pending.

`sudo /usr/lib/eitr/eitr-factory-reset status` (Walker → Reset Status) runs the
same checks and changes nothing.

## How a reset runs

The running root and home are never written. Under a new top-level subvolume
`@eitr-reset-previous` the helper:

1. Creates a writable snapshot of the restore point's root, recreates Snapper's
   `.snapshots` subvolume in it, copies in the current passwords and enables
   `eitr-factory-reset-finish.service` there.
2. Creates the new home: a writable snapshot of the restore point's home
   (Erase Everything), or a snapshot of the current `@home` with the settings
   moved aside as described above (Keep My Files).
3. Archives the current EFI partition files to `boot.tar` and unpacks the
   restore point's archive for copying.

A failure up to this point deletes `@eitr-reset-previous` and leaves the
computer unchanged. The helper then copies the restored boot files onto the EFI
partition (on failure it restores the archive it just made), renames `@` and
`@home` to `old@` and `old@home` inside `@eitr-reset-previous`, renames the
prepared subvolumes to `@` and `@home`, and restarts. If a rename fails, the
earlier names and boot files are restored.

On the next boot, `eitr-factory-reset-finish.service` confirms the running root
is the restored one, deletes `@eitr-reset-previous` (including the old
system's Snapper snapshots) and disables itself.

## Recovering an interrupted reset

Power loss during the few renames can leave `@` or `@home` missing. Boot the
Eitr ISO, press Escape to leave the wizard, unlock the disk if encrypted
(`cryptsetup open /dev/<partition> root`), and inspect:

```sh
mount -o subvolid=5 /dev/mapper/root /mnt   # or the Btrfs partition itself
btrfs subvolume list /mnt
cat /mnt/@eitr-reset-previous/manifest.json
```

- `@` and `@home` both exist and `@eitr-reset-previous/new-root` is gone: the
  swap finished. Reboot; the finish service cleans up.
- `@` or `@home` is missing: rename the matching `@eitr-reset-previous/old@`
  or `old@home` back (`mv /mnt/@eitr-reset-previous/old@ /mnt/@`), then extract
  `@eitr-reset-previous/boot.tar` onto the EFI partition to match the old
  system, and reboot.

Delete `@eitr-reset-previous` with `btrfs subvolume delete --recursive` only
after the system starts correctly; until then it holds the previous system.

## Verification

Tested in UEFI VMs without a network (see
[LINUX-VM-TESTING.md](LINUX-VM-TESTING.md)): both resets on an unencrypted
erase install, and both on a LUKS2 install next to a Windows-shaped disk, each
followed by a successful boot, login and the finish service's cleanup. Not yet
tested: real hardware, power loss during the swap, and restore point
retention through online system updates (the VMs had no network).

# Secure Boot with sbctl

Eitr documents Secure Boot but **never enrolls keys or signs files for you**.
A mistake here can leave a machine that refuses to boot or shows no picture, so
follow these steps by hand, on a machine you can reach firmware setup on, with
your disk passphrase and [recovery instructions](handbook:recovery) at hand. Nothing in
this guide has been verified on Eitr test hardware yet.

## Before you start

- UEFI boot only. Note how to open firmware setup (often F2, Del or F12) and set a
  firmware administrator password, or anyone can turn Secure Boot off again.
- If TPM disk unlock is enrolled, keep the passphrase ready: enrolling keys
  changes TPM PCR 7, so the next boot asks for it once. Re-enroll TPM unlock
  afterwards (Security → TPM Disk Unlock: remove, then enroll).
- In firmware setup, put Secure Boot into **Setup Mode** (often "Clear keys" or
  "Reset to Setup Mode"). Do not delete keys you cannot restore; most firmware has
  "Restore factory keys".

## sbctl workflow

```sh
sudo pacman -S --needed sbctl
sbctl status                      # must report "Setup Mode: Enabled"
sudo sbctl create-keys            # private keys stay in /var/lib/sbctl (root-only)
sudo sbctl enroll-keys -m         # -m keeps Microsoft's keys; see risks below
sudo sbctl verify                 # lists EFI files and whether they are signed
sudo sbctl sign -s <file>         # once per unsigned file listed by verify
```

`sign -s` saves the file in sbctl's database; sbctl's pacman hook re-signs saved
files after kernel and boot loader updates. Run `sudo sbctl verify` after each
change, then enable Secure Boot in firmware and reboot. Back up `/var/lib/sbctl`
offline and privately: it holds signing keys. Never copy it into this repository.

## Risks

- **Option ROMs and vendor keys.** Graphics cards, NVMe drives and network cards
  often run firmware (Option ROMs) signed by Microsoft's UEFI CA. Enrolling only
  your own keys without `-m` can make the firmware refuse them: no display, no
  boot disk, and on some laptops no way back into firmware setup. Keep `-m`
  unless you know the hardware has no such firmware. `sbctl enroll-keys
  --tpm-eventlog` can add the hashes of the Option ROMs used at this boot
  instead, but they change with hardware or firmware updates.
- **Unsigned files.** Every EFI binary in the boot path must be signed with your
  keys. A missed file stops the boot; disable Secure Boot in firmware to recover.

- **GRUB:** reinstall with

  booting, but the protection covers the GRUB binary rather than every kernel.

  hashes rather than signatures. If you enroll the config hash into the binary

  loader refuse its menu.

# Capture and sharing

Capture tools are under Main > Tools > Capture and Control Center > Tools.

## Screenshots and extraction

- **Print:** full screenshot in the floating editor.
- **SUPER + Print:** frozen selection in the floating editor.
- **SUPER + Shift + Print:** active-window screenshot in the editor.
- **SUPER + Ctrl + Print:** OCR text from a selection.
- **SUPER + Alt + Print:** decode a QR code from a selection.
- **SUPER + =:** pick a color and copy it.

A screenshot ends with a brief lightning flash that strikes what you captured.
It starts after the image is taken, so it never appears in the screenshot.

Review the selected content before saving or sharing. OCR results may be wrong;
QR codes can contain private credentials or untrusted URLs. A screenshot editor
is not a guarantee that sensitive background text has been removed.

Saved screenshots offer notification actions to open the image or its screenshots folder.

## Recording and streaming

Screen Recording opens OBS controls. They use your configured OBS scene and saved
Wayland capture permission; the scene must include a visible monitor source.
Starting capture prepares OBS and closes the panel before capture begins.
The controls use OBS's WebSocket, which OBS ships turned off: Eitr turns it on,
with a password, the first time while OBS is closed. If OBS is open then, close
it once and try again.
Recordings go to **Videos/Records** in your home folder. OBS's own default is
the home folder itself; Eitr changes only that default, so a folder you pick in
OBS > Settings > Output stays.
While OBS records or streams, a red dot sits beside the weather. Click it for the
elapsed time and file size, pause/resume, stop, a chapter marker (needs OBS's
Hybrid MP4 format), the OBS microphone and camera, and the scene; a stream shows
a LIVE timer with its own stop. When a recording stops, a notification offers
Open folder and Copy path. Check audio/mic choices
and the selected monitor before starting. Webcam requires an OBS camera source.
Recording audio switches affect OBS inputs, not your system volume.

The handbook never starts a recording or stream. Screen sharing and capture
remain explicit actions. Transcode offers the existing image/video conversion
workflow; review output paths before replacing a file.

OBS asks once which screen to record. In the standard share picker, **Allow restore token** is checked by default so OBS can remember your choice. The saved screen does not follow the bar’s Main display setting. Existing `~/.config/hypr/xdph.conf` files are kept, so your own portal settings may change this behavior.

For a new OBS configuration, Eitr creates an Untitled collection with one Scene: screen capture, a hidden camera, and default desktop and microphone audio. The system asks which screen to share on first use; OBS saves that permission. The camera stays off until you enable it. Existing collections are never changed.

## Share

Main > Tools > Share provides LocalSend and the existing transfer tools. Sending a file
requires choosing the destination/device. Verify recipients and avoid sharing
private keys, recovery codes, tokens or a complete unreviewed home/config folder.

# Development tools

Main > Development groups **AI**, **Cloud**, **Git Accounts**, **Monitoring**, **LazyVim** and
**VS Code**. Project selectors open the chosen directory in the editor; theme
integration updates supported open editors, including LazyVim sessions.

**Git Accounts** configures a default GitHub/GitLab identity, per-folder
overrides, SSH keys and separate provider CLI logins. Every rule change needs a
preview confirmation; it never rewrites project remotes or changes global CLI
accounts. See [Git Accounts](handbook:git-accounts).

## Optional toolchains

Install > Development Languages and JavaScript Tools install the tools you
choose. Java, Flutter and database clients are not required just to run EITR's
bar, launcher or themes. Install > Databases offers optional database tools.
Install > Developer Apps offers Bruno, Cursor, GitHub Desktop, Insomnia, JetBrains
Toolbox, Meld, Postman, VS Code and Zed; Install > Productivity offers
1Password, Bitwarden, Discord, LibreOffice, Obsidian, Slack and Thunderbird.
AUR entries download and build on your machine; some licenses do not allow
EITR to ship them.

## Web apps

Install > Web Apps > Create Web App asks for a name and an address and adds a
launcher that opens the site in its own window. The site's icon is downloaded
when you create it, only over HTTP(S). Malformed manifests or unavailable icons
fall back to page icons or a generic browser icon. Do not put login credentials
in the address. Launchers and icons use your XDG data directory, including a
custom `XDG_DATA_HOME`; removal through either menu uses that same location.
Web apps need Chrome, Chromium, Edge or Brave (Install > Browsers);
streaming sites with DRM, such as Netflix, need Chrome. Remove one with Delete
in Install > Web Apps or in the Apps menu.

Install > Browsers also offers Brave (AUR). Install > Productivity offers Basecamp and Notion as optional web apps. These recipes contain only a name and URL; the site icon is downloaded on your machine when you install. Nothing is preinstalled.

## AI assistants

Development > AI offers a menu for each installed assistant: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and GitHub Copilot CLI. Install them from Install > AI CLIs; with none installed, Development > AI links there.

Starting a session, or opening a LazyVim or VS Code project, first asks for a
folder under `~/Development`: pick folders to go deeper, Open to use the one
you are in, and Back to go up a level or, at the top, return to the menu.

Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and GitHub Copilot CLI (`copilot`) can also be started by command. If a tool is missing, Eitr explains it and offers the same installation as Install > AI CLIs. Type `yes` to install; Enter cancels. Without an interactive terminal, the command exits with installation instructions. Installed binaries take precedence over these launchers. Sign in through each tool’s own workflow; no assistant binaries or credentials are bundled.

Development > Default Assistant selects one installed assistant for this computer. **SUPER + Alt + A** opens it in a terminal; without a default, it opens the chooser. Eitr uses each assistant’s normal permission prompts.

Theme changes update only the light/dark theme setting in existing, readable Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Grok Build settings. Other settings and formatting stay intact. Missing, broken or uninstalled clients are skipped; assistants without a supported light/dark setting follow their terminal’s colors.

Installed SDK versions and installer sources are maintained in distro manifests.
Follow the actual picker rather than assuming a handbook example is a promise
about the newest upstream version. Toolchain installation may need downloads.

## Monitoring

Development > Monitoring keeps your dashboards one search away. **Add Dashboard**
asks for the service (Grafana, Datadog, Sentry, New Relic, Prometheus or Other),
a name and its address, and the dashboard then opens in your browser from the
menu. They are saved only on this computer, in `~/.config/eitr/monitoring.json`;
Delete removes one. Never put passwords or tokens in an address.

**Monitoring Tools** installs command-line tools: Prometheus's `promtool` and the
Sentry CLI. Amazon Managed Grafana workspaces are under Cloud > AWS > your
account > Grafana, with the other AWS tools.

## Accounts and cloud workflows

AI usage requires an installed/configured client; sign in through its normal
workflow. Account quotas and enterprise/API billing may differ from supported
personal-account panels. No credentials are bundled in EITR.

Cloud menus use your local provider accounts/profiles. AWS profiles come from
the local AWS configuration or configured EITR cloud profile mapping. Google
Cloud lists named gcloud configurations with their account and project. A
configuration without a project asks you to choose one when opening resource
tools, so Login remains accessible before project discovery. Azure lists enabled
subscriptions with their tenant IDs. Select a context before choosing a tool:
Google Cloud and Azure tools are searched inside their context menu, not from
global search. Opening a Google context clears unrelated inherited project
overrides; configurations without a project ask you to select one for resource
tools. Terminal returns retain the context, and the project you picked
for a configuration without one, without switching global CLI defaults. Login, Check Auth and
Refresh live inside each detected context. Google Login targets its configured
account; Azure Login targets its tenant and restores the previous default
subscription after authentication. Azure Refresh updates its subscription cache
and displays the selected subscription.

AWS accounts must have a matching `[default]` or `[profile NAME]` section in the AWS config file (`~/.aws/config`, or `AWS_CONFIG_FILE` when set). Profiles found only in the credentials file are excluded, as are config profiles that set `endpoint_url` (even an empty value), including nested service settings and referenced `[services NAME]` groups, because they may target S3-compatible services such as Cloudflare R2. `EITR_AWS_PROFILES` can label or restrict eligible profiles, but cannot include excluded ones. EITR does not edit either AWS file.

Each provider menu offers **Add AWS Account**, **Add GCP Account** or
**Add Azure Account**, so you can set up as many accounts as you need, for
example a company's Development and Production. It asks for a name first, then
runs the provider CLI's own setup under that name: an AWS profile through AWS SSO
(IAM Identity Center) or access keys, a separate gcloud configuration with its
sign-in and project, or an Azure sign-in whose subscriptions you name. A missing
`gcloud` or `az` is offered for installation first. **Ctrl+R** renames an account.
Names live in `~/.config/eitr/cloud-contexts.json` (keyed by AWS profile, gcloud
configuration or subscription ID); EITR does not infer environments or store
credentials there, and Add never switches a global CLI default. Grafana
and cloud operations need their corresponding accounts and permissions. Some
actions are read-only; others can modify remote resources—review the requested
operation and account before confirming.

Keep tokens, `.env` secrets and credentials outside shared dotfiles and
screenshots. Shell configuration loads supported managers without installers
rewriting your profiles. Learn retains dedicated LazyVim, tmux and cmux references.

## Assistants working together

Development > AI > Let assistants work together is off by default. Enable it
to connect installed Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Grok and Gemini CLI clients
that appear signed in. Each hand-off uses the helper's subscription or API
billing and counts toward its limits. Other clients' API-key-only and
keyring-only sign-ins are not detected.

Gemini is detected only with a non-empty `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY`,
or `security.auth.selectedType` set to `gemini-api-key` or `vertex-ai` in
`~/.gemini/settings.json`. Personal Google sign-in does not count: Google no
longer serves it. Gemini runs headlessly in plan mode, with MCP servers and
extensions excluded. It is not yet tested by Eitr; report problems with
Report a Problem. A real-account test remains open for a paid key or company
account. Plan mode is documented as read-only; Eitr has not independently
verified its file, shell or plan-file behavior.

Ask your assistant to consult the other one for a review, explanation or
suggestion. Approve each hand-off through the calling assistant’s normal tool
prompt; Eitr never pre-approves these tools. Do not enable automatic tool
approval for the assistants server. Helpers only read; edits stay with your
main assistant. A helper cannot ask another helper. A notification identifies
who asked whom, and each request has a three-minute timeout. The helper reads
the caller’s current working directory; its question and context may be sent
to that assistant’s provider.

The switch registers one `assistants` MCP server through each assistant's own
command (`claude mcp add`, `codex mcp add`, `copilot mcp add` and
`grok mcp add`, `gemini mcp add -s user`), so each assistant writes its own settings. An existing server with the same name is left unchanged
and reported. Changes
are recorded only on this computer in `~/.local/state/eitr/assistants.json`
(or `XDG_STATE_HOME`). Turning the switch off removes exactly Eitr’s entries;
if an entry was edited afterwards, Eitr keeps it and reports the conflict.
Restart existing assistant sessions after changing the switch. Real-account
hand-offs still await separate end-to-end verification.

Antigravity CLI (`agy`) is available for personal Google accounts through Install > AI CLIs and the first-use launcher. It is never bundled. It installs through Google's official installer, which verifies its download, and you sign in with your Google account. It is not yet offered as an assistants-together helper. An already installed `agy` can be launched normally. Gemini CLI requires a Gemini API key or a Google Cloud/company account. Antigravity is not a collaboration helper: headless mode denies even reads. Its only unlocks bypass permissions or change global rules. Eitr will reconsider it when per-run permissions or a read-only headless mode are available.

### Additional providers

Development > Cloud also lists Cloudflare (`wrangler`), DigitalOcean (`doctl`), Hetzner Cloud (`hcloud`), Oracle Cloud (`oci`), Vercel, Netlify and IBM Cloud (`ibmcloud`). Add an account using a lowercase name with digits or dashes. These accounts are private workspaces under `~/.config/eitr/cloud-accounts/<provider>/<name>`; existing provider configurations are never imported. The chosen provider and workspace remain visible in the tool picker and terminal. Return from a terminal to the same workspace; Shift+Backspace returns to the account list. Selecting a workspace never switches a global CLI default.

Missing `wrangler`, `doctl` and `hcloud` are offered from Arch's official repositories (`doctl` and `hcloud` in extra). Oracle Cloud and IBM Cloud use their official HTTPS shell installers from `distro/installers.json`; Oracle passes `--accept-all-defaults`. Vercel (`vercel`) and Netlify (`netlify-cli`, command `netlify`) use the existing NVM/npm installation recipe. Installation requires confirmation. Sign-in and account actions run only inside the selected private workspace. DigitalOcean and Hetzner list native contexts; Oracle lists profiles from that workspace's `~/.oci/config`. Selecting their context/profile saves a local selection and uses per-command flags, without changing a global default. Vercel and Netlify expose their native switch action; enter the selected team/account label afterward. Vercel also asks for a scope before login and passes `--scope TEAM` on subsequent commands. IBM provides SSO and API-key sign-in, displays `ibmcloud target`, and targets an explicit account and region. The selected context/profile/scope/account and saved region remain visible when returning to the menu. These labels are local selections, not verified remote identities. Existing credentials and provider overrides are not inherited. Browser consoles use their own sessions; check the account before acting.

The seven private-workspace providers use neutral resource and action icons with short descriptions. Accounts appear first in alphabetical order, followed by Add Account; tools are sorted alphabetically by their translated names. The picker shows the selected account, context and saved region, and each read-only report repeats that context above its output. Reports retain the shared AWS pager; no additional resource commands or log searches are introduced.

| Provider | Sign in | List / switch / command context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloudflare | `wrangler login` | — |
| DigitalOcean | `doctl auth init --context NAME` | `doctl auth list`; `doctl auth switch --context NAME`; `--context NAME` |
| Hetzner Cloud | `hcloud context create NAME` | `hcloud context list`; `hcloud context use NAME`; `--context NAME` |
| Oracle Cloud | `oci session authenticate --profile-name NAME --region REGION` | `~/.oci/config`; `--profile NAME --auth security_token` |
| Vercel | `vercel login` | `vercel switch`; `--scope TEAM` |
| Netlify | `netlify login` | `netlify switch` |
| IBM Cloud | `ibmcloud login --sso`; `ibmcloud login --apikey` | `ibmcloud target`; `ibmcloud target -c ACCOUNT -r REGION` |

Cloud navigation uses real Elephant menus. Shift+Backspace goes to the previous menu: a service or resource choice returns to its containing menu, the account menu returns to the provider’s account list, and that list returns to Cloud. The selected account and context remain visible. Eitr stores this navigation selection in `~/.config/eitr/cloud-navigation.json`; provider CLI defaults stay unchanged. Reports keep their pager, log searches keep fzf, and setup keeps its reviewed terminal forms. Free-text search prompts still accept text in Walker; they are not navigation lists.

Delete an account with the Delete key on its account row or **Delete Account** inside its menu. The confirmation names the provider and account: it removes that provider’s sign-in for that account on this computer, without affecting the remote account. Cancellation changes nothing. Only the selected Eitr private account folder is removed; symbolic links, paths outside its provider root and accounts with a running Eitr action are refused. AWS, Azure and Google Cloud have no new deletion action. The confirmation opens inside Walker with Cancel and Confirm; no terminal opens.

Read-only reports use the selected private account environment and the existing cloud pager. Cloudflare: Account, R2 Buckets, D1 Databases, KV Namespaces, Pages Projects, Queues. DigitalOcean: Droplets, Apps, Databases, Kubernetes, Volumes, Domains, Load Balancers, Balance. Hetzner: Servers, Volumes, Networks, Firewalls, Load Balancers, Primary IPs, Snapshots. Oracle: Compartments, Instances, Buckets, VCNs. Vercel: Projects, Deployments, Domains. Netlify: Status, Sites. IBM: Account, Target, Resource Groups, Service Instances. DigitalOcean and Hetzner always pass the chosen context; Oracle passes the chosen profile and security-token authentication, reading the tenancy only from that account’s private profile. Bucket listing first reads its namespace. Vercel passes the selected team scope. Errors remain readable and never trigger a retry with another account. Log searches retain the existing fzf viewer. Live checks with real accounts remain pending.

Setup forms for cloud accounts, Git Accounts (Add and Edit), monitoring dashboards and web apps list their steps on the left and the current answer on the right. Use arrows or Tab to select a step and Enter to answer it. Review lists every answer before applying anything; return to a step with Left or the arrows, and use PgUp/PgDn to scroll long reviews. Esc or Ctrl+C cancels without saving. Vendor sign-in starts after review; failed or interrupted sign-in discards the new account. Google Cloud asks for an optional project ID before sign-in; Azure asks for an optional subscription label before sign-in and otherwise keeps each subscription’s existing name. Vercel asks for its scope before sign-in.

Theme changes update only the light/dark theme setting in existing, readable Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Grok Build settings. Other settings and formatting stay intact. Missing, broken or uninstalled clients are skipped; assistants without a supported light/dark setting follow their terminal’s colors.

Installed SDK versions and installer sources are maintained in distro manifests. Follow the actual picker rather than assuming a handbook example is a promise about the newest upstream version. Toolchain installation may need downloads.
Monitoring

Development > Monitoring keeps your dashboards one search away. Add Dashboard asks for the service (Grafana, Datadog, Sentry, New Relic, Prometheus or Other), a name and its address, and the dashboard then opens in your browser from the menu. They are saved only on this computer, in ~/.config/eitr/monitoring.json; Delete removes one. Never put passwords or tokens in an address.
Monitoring Tools installs command-line tools: Prometheus's promtool and the Sentry CLI. Amazon Managed Grafana workspaces are under Cloud > AWS > your account > Grafana, with the other AWS tools.
Accounts and cloud workflows

AI usage requires an installed/configured client; sign in through its normal workflow. Account quotas and enterprise/API billing may differ from supported personal-account panels. No credentials are bundled in EITR.

Cloud menus use your local provider accounts/profiles. AWS profiles come from the local AWS configuration or configured EITR cloud profile mapping. Google Cloud lists named gcloud configurations with their account and project. A configuration without a project asks you to choose one when opening resource tools, so Login remains accessible before project discovery. Azure lists enabled subscriptions with their tenant IDs. Select a context before choosing a tool: Google Cloud and Azure tools are searched inside their context menu, not from global search. Opening a Google context clears unrelated inherited project overrides; configurations without a project ask you to select one for resource tools. Terminal returns retain the context, and the project you picked for a configuration without one, without switching global CLI defaults. Login, Check Auth and Refresh live inside each detected context. Google Login targets its configured account; Azure Login targets its tenant and restores the previous default subscription after authentication. Azure Refresh updates its subscription cache and displays the selected subscription.

AWS accounts must have a matching [default] or [profile NAME] section in the AWS config file (~/.aws/config, or AWS_CONFIG_FILE when set). Profiles found only in the credentials file are excluded, as are config profiles that set endpoint_url (even an empty value), including nested service settings and referenced [services NAME] groups, because they may target S3-compatible services such as Cloudflare R2. Each provider menu offers Add AWS Account, Add GCP Account or Add Azure Account, so you can set up as many accounts as you need, for example a company's Development and Production. It asks for a name first, then runs the provider CLI's own setup under that name: an AWS profile through AWS SSO (IAM Identity Center) or access keys, a separate gcloud configuration with its sign-in and project, or an Azure sign-in whose subscriptions you name. A missing gcloud or az is offered for installation first. Ctrl+R renames an account. Names live in ~/.config/eitr/cloud-contexts.json (keyed by AWS profile, gcloud configuration or subscription ID); EITR does not infer environments or store credentials there, and Add never switches a global CLI default. Grafana and cloud operations need their corresponding accounts and permissions. Some actions are read-only; others can modify remote resources—review the requested operation and account before confirming.

Keep tokens, .env secrets and credentials outside shared dotfiles and screenshots. Shell configuration loads supported managers without installers rewriting your profiles. Learn retains dedicated LazyVim, tmux and cmux references.

Development > AI > Let assistants work together is off by default. Enable it to connect installed Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Grok and Gemini CLI clients that appear signed in. Each hand-off uses the helper's subscription or API billing and counts toward its limits. Other clients' API-key-only and keyring-only sign-ins are not detected.

Gemini is detected only with a non-empty GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY, or security.auth.selectedType set to gemini-api-key or vertex-ai in ~/.gemini/settings.json. Personal Google sign-in does not count: Google no longer serves it. Gemini runs headlessly in plan mode, with MCP servers and extensions excluded. It is not yet tested by Eitr; report problems with Report a Problem. A real-account test remains open for a paid key or company account. Plan mode is documented as read-only; Eitr has not independently verified its file, shell or plan-file behavior.

Do not enable automatic tool approval for the assistants server. Helpers only read; edits stay with your main assistant. A helper cannot ask another helper. The helper reads the caller’s current working directory; its question and context may be sent to that assistant’s provider.

The switch registers one assistants MCP server through each assistant's own command (claude mcp add, codex mcp add, copilot mcp add and grok mcp add, gemini mcp add -s user), so each assistant writes its own settings. An existing server with the same name is left unchanged and reported. Changes are recorded only on this computer in ~/.local/state/eitr/assistants.json (or XDG_STATE_HOME). Turning the switch off removes exactly Eitr’s entries; if an entry was edited afterwards, Eitr keeps it and reports the conflict. Restart existing assistant sessions after changing the switch. Real-account hand-offs still await separate end-to-end verification.

Antigravity CLI (agy) is available for personal Google accounts through Install > AI CLIs and the first-use launcher. It is never bundled. Add an account using a lowercase name with digits or dashes. These accounts are private workspaces under ~/.config/eitr/cloud-accounts/<provider>/<name>; existing provider configurations are never imported. IBM provides SSO and API-key sign-in, displays ibmcloud target, and targets an explicit account and region. Existing credentials and provider overrides are not inherited. Browser consoles use their own sessions; check the account before acting.

The seven private-workspace providers use neutral resource and action icons with short descriptions. Accounts appear first in alphabetical order, followed by Add Account; tools are sorted alphabetically by their translated names. The picker shows the selected account, context and saved region, and each read-only report repeats that context above its output. Reports retain the shared AWS pager; no additional resource commands or log searches are introduced.

Provider Sign in List / switch / command context
Cloudflare wrangler login —
DigitalOcean doctl auth init --context NAME doctl auth list; doctl auth switch --context NAME; --context NAME
Hetzner Cloud hcloud context create NAME hcloud context list; hcloud context use NAME; --context NAME
Oracle Cloud oci session authenticate --profile-name NAME --region REGION ~/.oci/config; --profile NAME --auth security_token
Vercel vercel login vercel switch; --scope TEAM
Netlify netlify login netlify switch
IBM Cloud ibmcloud login --sso; ibmcloud login --apikey ibmcloud target; ibmcloud target -c ACCOUNT -r REGION

Cloud navigation uses real Elephant menus. Shift+Backspace goes to the previous menu: a service or resource choice returns to its containing menu, the account menu returns to the provider’s account list, and that list returns to Cloud. The selected account and context remain visible. Eitr stores this navigation selection in ~/.config/eitr/cloud-navigation.json; provider CLI defaults stay unchanged. Reports keep their pager, log searches keep fzf, and setup keeps its reviewed terminal forms. Free-text search prompts still accept text in Walker; they are not navigation lists.

Delete an account with the Delete key on its account row or Delete Account inside its menu. The confirmation names the provider and account: it removes that provider’s sign-in for that account on this computer, without affecting the remote account. Cancellation changes nothing. Only the selected Eitr private account folder is removed; symbolic links, paths outside its provider root and accounts with a running Eitr action are refused. AWS, Azure and Google Cloud have no new deletion action. The confirmation opens inside Walker with Cancel and Confirm; no terminal opens.

Read-only reports use the selected private account environment and the existing cloud pager. Cloudflare: Account, R2 Buckets, D1 Databases, KV Namespaces, Pages Projects, Queues. DigitalOcean: Droplets, Apps, Databases, Kubernetes, Volumes, Domains, Load Balancers, Balance. Hetzner: Servers, Volumes, Networks, Firewalls, Load Balancers, Primary IPs, Snapshots. Oracle: Compartments, Instances, Buckets, VCNs. Vercel: Projects, Deployments, Domains. Netlify: Status, Sites. IBM: Account, Target, Resource Groups, Service Instances. DigitalOcean and Hetzner always pass the chosen context; Oracle passes the chosen profile and security-token authentication, reading the tenancy only from that account’s private profile. Bucket listing first reads its namespace. Vercel passes the selected team scope. Errors remain readable and never trigger a retry with another account. Log searches retain the existing fzf viewer. Live checks with real accounts remain pending.

Setup forms for cloud accounts, Git Accounts (Add and Edit), monitoring dashboards and web apps list their steps on the left and the current answer on the right. Use arrows or Tab to select a step and Enter to answer it. Review lists every answer before applying anything; return to a step with Left or the arrows, and use PgUp/PgDn to scroll long reviews. Esc or Ctrl+C cancels without saving. Vendor sign-in starts after review; failed or interrupted sign-in discards the new account. Google Cloud asks for an optional project ID before sign-in; Azure asks for an optional subscription label before sign-in and otherwise keeps each subscription’s existing name. Vercel asks for its scope before sign-in.

# Terminal and editors

**SUPER + Enter** opens Kitty. **SUPER + Ctrl + Enter** opens/attaches the main
tmux session. **SUPER + P** fuzzy-finds files; **SUPER + Ctrl + P** searches file
contents. Learn > Cmux Commands, Tmux Commands and LazyVim Commands are
searchable references; selecting a command copies it, rather than executing it.

Kitty shows a short cursor trail on jumps of at least two cells, such as
Enter, Home/End and moving between words. It starts after the cursor has rested
for 3 ms and fades in 0.05–0.15 seconds. To customize it, set `cursor_trail`,
`cursor_trail_decay` or `cursor_trail_start_threshold` in
`~/.config/kitty/local.conf`; `cursor_trail 0` disables it. Personal options
override the packaged defaults and survive theme changes.

### Cursor Fire

**Style > Terminal > Cursor Fire** offers **Disabled** (the default) and
**Enabled**. Enabled selects Kitty's built-in `cursor-trail-blaze` effect on
cursor movements, with no typing-speed detection. Disabled returns to the
normal configured fast trail and any personal shader selection.

The effect needs Kitty 0.49+ and `shader-slang`, included in Eitr's desktop
dependencies. Enabling validates the built-in shader before saving or reloading
Kitty. The machine-local preference is `~/.config/eitr/terminal.json`; the helper
writes `kitty/cursor-fire.conf`, included last by Kitty's user loader. While
enabled, it selects the fire shader and lowers the movement threshold to one
cell. Fonts, themes and personal config files remain intact.

## The eitr command

`eitr` gathers Eitr's tools in one command; run it alone for the list. It runs the
same scripts as the menus, so both always behave alike.

```
eitr update                  # System Update: snapshot, packages, AUR, Flatpak
eitr update aur              # only AUR packages, without a snapshot
eitr theme list              # installed themes, the current one marked *
eitr theme set "Norse" # switch theme
eitr firewall on             # also: off, status
eitr snapshots               # recovery snapshots
eitr snapshots changes       # what each update changed
eitr reset keep-files        # factory reset, after the usual two warnings
eitr report                  # prepare a problem report
eitr handbook troubleshooting
eitr version
```

`eitr config` and `eitr git` pass their arguments to `eitr-config` and `eitr-git`.
Each command has `--help`.

## Your own hooks

A hook is a small script of yours that Eitr runs at a certain moment, so you can
add to what it does without changing Eitr itself. Put an executable file named
after the moment in `~/.config/eitr/hooks/`:

| File | Runs | Gets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `post-update` | after System Update or a pacman/AUR update | `system`, `pacman`, `yay` or `full` |
| `theme-set` | after switching theme | the theme's folder name |
| `battery-low` | once each time the battery drops to 15% | the percentage |
| `post-boot` | at the first login after each start | nothing |

For example, to recolor Spotify (with Spicetify) whenever the theme changes,
create `~/.config/eitr/hooks/theme-set`:

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
spicetify config color_scheme "$1" && spicetify apply
```

then make it executable with `chmod +x ~/.config/eitr/hooks/theme-set`. Each hook
gets up to 60 seconds; its output and any failure go to
`~/.local/state/eitr/hooks.log`, and a failing hook never stops the update or
theme switch. `eitr hook list` shows which hooks exist, and
`eitr hook run theme-set norse` tries one. Updates never touch this folder.

## cmux TUI

Run `cmux` in Kitty, or `cmux --session work` for a named session. cmux TUI
is an optional workflow alongside tmux, not a replacement for Kitty or its
existing shortcuts. Fresh EITR installs include a pinned official binary at
`/usr/bin/cmux`; existing per-user installs may take precedence on PATH.
Use `command -v cmux` to see which one is selected. `less` is included for
reading terminal output and text files.

The default prefix is **Ctrl-b**: release it, then press the next key.

| Shortcut | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl-b ? | Show current shortcuts |
| Ctrl-b W | Create workspace |
| Ctrl-b c | Create screen |
| Ctrl-b % / Ctrl-b " | Split right / down |
| Ctrl-b t | New terminal tab |
| Ctrl-b h/j/k/l | Focus left/down/up/right |
| Ctrl-b s | Show/hide sidebar |
| Ctrl-b d | Quit locally or detach from a server |

For a session that continues without the UI, run
`cmux --headless --session work`, then `cmux attach --session work` to attach.
Browser tabs require Chrome/Chromium. Closing tabs, panes or workspaces may
affect running tasks; check before using those actions. Learn > Cmux Commands
includes session commands, navigation, mouse controls and closing shortcuts.
Defaults can change or be overridden; **Ctrl-b ?** is the live reference.

## Task terminals

Terminals that menus open, and the update and problem-report notifications'
terminals, float centered above your windows and use the theme's solid background. AI assistant sessions and LazyVim projects (Development menu)
open as ordinary tiled windows, like terminals you open yourself, with the
translucent background.
Ordinary terminals are interactive and unbranded. Installer/update/setup
terminals show the themed rune-style EITR banner; successful tasks normally
close, and failures stay open until dismissed. Informational reports may stay
open intentionally. Restarting Elephant is not supposed to close launched apps:
its systemd service uses process-only stopping, not whole-cgroup termination.

Press **Esc** to close waiting task, account, report and About terminals. Enter remains for answers and confirmations, including acknowledging a recovery key and powering off the installer.

## Shell history

`history` lists recent commands. In zsh, inspect the actual history path with:

```sh
printf '%s\n' "$HISTFILE"
```

To open it in Neovim:

```sh
nvim "$HISTFILE"
```

History may contain tokens or credentials; do not copy it into a bug report.
Close other shells before manually editing it, because running shells can
write their in-memory history back. Extended zsh history can include timestamp
metadata and multiline commands; remove the whole relevant entry, not an
arbitrary fragment. Back it up privately if you need an undo.

## Editor appearance

Theme changes update generated VS Code and LazyVim preferences. Supported live
LazyVim sessions refresh without reopening. User overrides/plugins can choose
their own colors; verify their configuration if an editor does not follow the
desktop. Default-font integration is applied only where the app supports it.

chapters.title: Troubleshooting
chapters.summary: Missing helpers, service restarts, dependencies, installation checks and backups
chapters.markdown:
# Troubleshooting

## A menu action reports a missing tool

Fresh distro manifests include desktop runtime dependencies, but an existing
Arch desktop may lack some. Read the exact error and install the corresponding
package through Install > Packages > Pacman or a normal full-system update. Do not remove
BlueZ/iwd/PipeWire/WirePlumber merely because their settings are in native panels:
the panels still need those backends.

This handbook does not need `less`. It is bundled Markdown in a native overlay.
If the reader reports a missing/stale catalog, update the EITR desktop files.

## Root-owned helper missing

Network switching, security, battery limits and recovery operations require
reviewed root-owned helpers. A dotfiles-only desktop may not have the packaged
helpers yet. See the relevant chapter; never work around the check by running a
user-writable downloaded helper as root. The selector must not disconnect your
network just because you opened it.

## Configuration or service problems

Quickshell shows a readable reload error and retains the previous working
configuration when possible. Fix the named file; do not repeatedly restart the
login manager. **Never restart SDDM during your desktop session.**

An Elephant restart reloads menu definitions. Its service must retain
`KillMode=process` so launched apps survive. Themes regenerate styles, so fix
the generator as well as generated output if a change disappears later.

## Installation and recovery checks

EITR is still in beta: VM coverage does not prove every WiFi adapter, Bluetooth
pairing agent, TPM, GPU, fingerprint reader or Secure Boot setup works. Current
backend/enterprise WiFi code is mock-tested; test real authentication before
depending on it. Existing ISO files do not change when repository manifests
change: rebuild the payload/ISO for those changes to reach a new installation.

Back up your other disks before installing to a spare SSD and verify the target
disk carefully. The installer erases the disk you confirm. Keep encryption
passphrases and recovery keys offline. Snapshots on that same SSD are not an
independent backup. Start with [Recovery & Snapshots](handbook:recovery).

## Reporting a problem

**System > Information > Report a Problem** collects the EITR and package
versions, graphics hardware, Hyprland errors, failed services, recent warnings,
crashes of the last week, errors from the previous start, the installation log
and recent package changes into `~/Documents/eitr-problem-report-<time>.txt`,
readable only by you. It removes your user name, computer name, home path,
email, IP and MAC addresses, but logs can still mention apps or file names: read
it before sending it.

Nothing is sent by itself, and the terminal shows only where the report was
saved. It then offers ways to send it, or to read it first:

1. **Email** to `reports@eitr.info`: your email app opens a message with a short
   summary; attach the saved file.
2. **GitHub issue** (needs a GitHub account): the browser opens a new issue on
   the Eitr project. Issues are public.
3. **Copy** the report to paste anywhere.
4. **Read** the report: it opens in your text editor.

A report is used only to find and fix the problem, and is deleted once it is
fixed. An email shares your email address; reply to it to have your report
deleted at any time.

### When something crashes

Crash Notifications are on by default. A user service watches new, readable systemd-coredump records for your own programs. Each crash offers Report a problem, Ignore, and Mute this program; Ask the AI appears when a default assistant is installed and selected. Repeated crashes of one program are limited to one notification every five minutes. Toggle Crash Notifications under Main > Toggle or Control Center > Quick Toggles. Preferences and muted program paths stay in `~/.config/eitr/crash-help.json`; remove a path from `ignored` to allow it again.

Ask the AI opens your default assistant with only the program, signal and backtrace from `coredumpctl info`, asking for an explanation and a proposed fix without changing the system unless you agree. No core dump is passed. Your assistant may send that summary to its provider when you choose this action. Report a problem attaches the same summary to the existing report workflow: review it before sharing; nothing is sent automatically.

## Customizations and updates

EITR's own code is installed under `/usr/share/eitr` and updated with the
`eitr-desktop` package; your settings stay in `~/.config`. Put lasting changes
where updates never touch them:

- Monitors, devices, extra bindings and rules: `~/.config/hypr/local.lua`.
- Shell additions: `~/.config/eitr/shell.local.zsh`.
- Terminal options: `~/.config/kitty/local.conf`.
- Launcher colors: `~/.config/walker/style.override.css`.
- A whole replacement for a shipped file: the same relative path under
  `~/.config/eitr/overrides`. It no longer receives fixes from updates.

Theme files such as `kitty/theme.conf` and the Walker style are regenerated when
you switch themes and once after each package update; the previous copies are
kept under `~/.local/state/eitr/generated-backups`. When an update changes how a
setting is stored, it is converted once at login; a failure is reported and
retried at the next login (`~/.local/state/eitr/migrations.log`).
`eitr-config status` lists the settings and overrides in effect.

Root-owned helper missing

Network switching, security, battery limits and recovery operations require reviewed root-owned helpers. A dotfiles-only desktop may not have the packaged helpers yet. See the relevant chapter; never work around the check by running a user-writable downloaded helper as root. The selector must not disconnect your network just because you opened it.
Configuration or service problems

Quickshell shows a readable reload error and retains the previous working configuration when possible. Fix the named file; do not repeatedly restart the login manager. Never restart SDDM during your desktop session.

An Elephant restart reloads menu definitions. Its service must retain KillMode=process so launched apps survive. Themes regenerate styles, so fix the generator as well as generated output if a change disappears later.
Installation and recovery checks

EITR is still in beta: VM coverage does not prove every WiFi adapter, Bluetooth pairing agent, TPM, GPU, fingerprint reader or Secure Boot setup works. Current backend/enterprise WiFi code is mock-tested; test real authentication before depending on it. Existing ISO files do not change when repository manifests change: rebuild the payload/ISO for those changes to reach a new installation.

Back up your other disks before installing to a spare SSD and verify the target disk carefully. The installer erases the disk you confirm. Keep encryption passphrases and recovery keys offline. Snapshots on that same SSD are not an independent backup. Start with Recovery & Snapshots.
Reporting a problem

System > Information > Report a Problem collects the EITR and package versions, graphics hardware, Hyprland errors, failed services, recent warnings, crashes of the last week, errors from the previous start, the installation log and recent package changes into ~/Documents/eitr-problem-report-<time>.txt, readable only by you. It removes your user name, computer name, home path, email, IP and MAC addresses, but logs can still mention apps or file names: read it before sending it.
Nothing is sent by itself, and the terminal shows only where the report was saved. It then offers ways to send it, or to read it first:

1. Email to reports@eitr.info: your email app opens a message with a short summary; attach the saved file.
  2. GitHub issue (needs a GitHub account): the browser opens a new issue on the Eitr project. Issues are public.
  3. Copy the report to paste anywhere.
  4. Read the report: it opens in your text editor.
A report is used only to find and fix the problem, and is deleted once it is fixed. An email shares your email address; reply to it to have your report deleted at any time.
When something crashes

Crash Notifications are on by default. A user service watches new, readable systemd-coredump records for your own programs. Each crash offers Report a problem, Ignore, and Mute this program; Ask the AI appears when a default assistant is installed and selected. Repeated crashes of one program are limited to one notification every five minutes. Toggle Crash Notifications under Main > Toggle or Control Center > Quick Toggles. Preferences and muted program paths stay in ~/.config/eitr/crash-help.json; remove a path from ignored to allow it again.

Ask the AI opens your default assistant with only the program, signal and backtrace from coredumpctl info, asking for an explanation and a proposed fix without changing the system unless you agree. No core dump is passed. Your assistant may send that summary to its provider when you choose this action. Report a problem attaches the same summary to the existing report workflow: review it before sharing; nothing is sent automatically.
Customizations and updates
EITR's own code is installed under /usr/share/eitr and updated with the eitr-desktop package; your settings stay in ~/.config. Put lasting changes where updates never touch them:

• Monitors, devices, extra bindings and rules: ~/.config/hypr/local.lua.
  • Shell additions: ~/.config/eitr/shell.local.zsh.
  • Terminal options: ~/.config/kitty/local.conf.
  • Launcher colors: ~/.config/walker/style.override.css.
  • A whole replacement for a shipped file: the same relative path under ~/.config/eitr/overrides. It no longer receives fixes from updates.

Theme files such as kitty/theme.conf and the Walker style are regenerated when you switch themes and once after each package update; the previous copies are kept under ~/.local/state/eitr/generated-backups. When an update changes how a setting is stored, it is converted once at login; a failure is reported and retried at the next login (~/.local/state/eitr/migrations.log). eitr-config status lists the settings and overrides in effect.

# Language

Eitr follows the system's message locale. **Control Center > System > Language**
shows the language Eitr uses for that locale and opens a language picker;
**Walker > System > Language** lists the same choices with the current one
checked. Choose a language or **System default**,
then sign out and back in. Eitr never signs you out automatically.

Eitr checks **LC_ALL**, then **LC_MESSAGES**, then **LANG**. Empty variables are
ignored. `LC_MESSAGES` changes messages without changing your date, number or
currency formats; `LC_ALL` overrides all locale categories and is normally left
unset. `C`, `POSIX` and unsupported languages use English. A missing translated
message falls back to English; a missing Handbook chapter falls back as a whole.

## Change the system language

The picker writes only `~/.config/environment.d/90-eitr-language.conf`. It sets
`LC_MESSAGES` and clears `LC_ALL` for the next user session, preserving your
date and number formats. **System default** removes that preference. It never
edits `/etc/locale.conf` or generates locales. If necessary, use your system locale configuration. On Arch Linux, enable the locale you want
in `/etc/locale.gen` and regenerate installed locales with `sudo locale-gen`.
Then set the language in `/etc/locale.conf`, for example:

```text
LANG=pt_BR.UTF-8
```

The first translation targets are `pt_BR.UTF-8` (Brazilian Portuguese),
`es_ES.UTF-8` (Spanish), `de_DE.UTF-8` (German) and `fr_FR.UTF-8` (French).
Regional variants can fall back to the base language. Check `locale` in a
terminal for overrides, and `locale -a` for installed locales. Sign out and back
in to apply the language to the desktop, menus and newly opened terminals.
The picker changes your next session; already running applications keep their language.

## Contribute a translation

English text is the source. Catalogs live in `i18n/catalogs/<locale>/`; edit the
translated values, keeping the English keys. Python and shell messages use the
single `eitr` gettext domain. Keep placeholders such as `%1` and `{name}`, glyphs,
package names, commands and file paths unchanged. Typed destructive-action
confirmation words must match the words the confirmation check accepts.

Handbook chapters go in
`quickshell/desktop-bar/handbook/content/<locale>/<chapter-id>.md`. Keep
`handbook:` links, code blocks and commands intact. Keyboard and mouse tables
are generated from the canonical shortcut sources; translate their messages in
the Handbook catalog rather than maintaining a second list of bindings.

Run `python3 tools/i18n-build.py --check`, rebuild the Handbook with
`python3 quickshell/desktop-bar/scripts/handbook-build.py`, then run its `--check`
and `bash tools/check.sh`. Catalog checks list missing messages and changed
placeholders. Check long translations in offscreen previews before submitting.

After translating a changed chapter in full, update its entry in `source-hashes.json` with the SHA-256 of the English source. The build check flags changed or unrecorded English sources; rebuilding catalogs alone never acknowledges a source change.

The System default row shows the native name resolved from `/etc/locale.conf`: `LC_ALL`, then `LC_MESSAGES`, then `LANG`, ignoring empty values. It ignores session overrides. English forces English; System default follows the system. If the system locale cannot be read, the row keeps its plain label.

The fixed language matching System default is hidden unless it is your saved explicit choice, so the current choice stays visible. If the system default cannot be resolved, all languages remain listed.
